listening.title: The history and science of glass
listening.titleVi: Lịch sử và khoa học của nghề làm thủy tinh
listening.context: A lecturer gives a talk on how glass is made and how glass-making developed.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history and science of glass-making. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning. Today we're looking at a material we hardly ever notice, even though we look through it all day: glass.
I'll start with what glass is actually made of, then go through some key moments in its history, and finish with a little of the science.
So, the ingredients. The main ingredient in almost all glass, both ancient and modern, is sand – or, more precisely, the silica in sand.
The difficulty is that pure silica only melts at around seventeen hundred degrees, which was far too hot for any early furnace.
Even a good charcoal fire in the ancient world could only reach about eleven hundred degrees, so something else was needed.
So early glass-makers added soda, which lowers the melting point considerably. In many coastal regions, this soda came from burnt seaweed.
But glass made from just sand and soda has a serious weakness: it slowly dissolves in water. Not very useful for a drinking cup!
The third ingredient, lime, solves this. It makes the glass chemically stable, so it can hold liquids for centuries.
Let's turn to the history. People have used natural glass, such as volcanic obsidian, for tools since prehistoric times.
But the earliest man-made glass objects we know of come from Mesopotamia, around 2500 BC. They weren't vessels or windows.
They were beads – small, brightly coloured, and very valuable. Glass was treated almost like a precious stone.
For the next two thousand years, glass stayed a luxury, because shaping it was slow. It was usually formed around a core of clay.
The real turning point came in the first century BC, somewhere on the eastern Mediterranean coast, with the invention of glassblowing.
With a simple metal pipe, a skilled worker could produce a bottle in minutes. Within a few generations, glass became cheap enough for ordinary families.
The Roman Empire spread the technique across Europe, and glass bottles and cups became normal household items.
The Romans were also the first to put glass into windows, although it was thick and cloudy, more to let light in than to see through.
Jumping forward to medieval Venice, which became the centre of fine glass-making. In 1291, the city ordered all its glass workshops to move to the island of Murano.
Some people say this was to protect trade secrets, and that did become important later.
But the original reason was the risk of fire. Furnaces burning day and night in a city of wooden buildings were simply too dangerous.
Murano's craftsmen are famous for a very clear glass called cristallo. Ordinary glass has a slightly green tint, caused by iron in the sand.
To remove this colour, the Venetians added small amounts of manganese, which is why glass-makers sometimes called it 'glassmaker's soap'.
Now, the science. Why is glass transparent, and what kind of material is it? Most solids, such as metals or salt, are crystals.
Their atoms are arranged in a regular, repeating pattern. Glass is different. When it cools, the atoms are frozen in place before they can form that pattern.
And because there are no crystal boundaries inside it to scatter light, light passes straight through. That's what makes glass transparent.
That's why scientists call it an amorphous solid – 'amorphous' meaning 'without shape'.
This leads to a popular myth. You may have heard that glass is really a very slow liquid, and that's why old church windows are thicker at the bottom.
In fact, at room temperature, glass wouldn't flow measurably in millions of years. The real explanation is the way the windows were made.
Early window panes were never perfectly even, and the glaziers who fitted them usually put the thicker edge at the bottom, because that was more stable.
Finally, a word on modern windows. Since the 1950s, almost all flat glass has been made by the float process.
Molten glass is poured onto a bath of liquid tin. Because the tin is perfectly flat, the glass spreads out and cools into a perfectly smooth sheet.
Before this, sheets had to be ground and polished by hand or by machine, which was slow and wasted a great deal of glass.
The float process made large, cheap windows possible, and you can see the result in every glass office tower built since then.
Next week, we'll look at how glass is being recycled, and why that is harder than it sounds.

groups.title: Glass-making: history and science
groups.instr: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

items.cue: is sand
items.explain: Giảng viên nói thành phần chính “is sand – or, more precisely, the silica in sand”. Đáp án là sand.

items.text: Soda lowers the melting point; often obtained from burnt ___
items.cue: this soda came from burnt seaweed
items.explain: “In many coastal regions, this soda came from burnt seaweed”. Đề lặp lại gần như nguyên văn cụm “burnt ___”, đáp án là seaweed.

items.text: Without lime, glass gradually dissolves in ___
items.cue: it slowly dissolves in water
items.explain: Thủy tinh chỉ có cát và soda “slowly dissolves in water” (slowly = gradually); vôi (lime) khắc phục điều này. Đáp án là water.

items.cue: They were beads
items.explain: Đồ thủy tinh nhân tạo sớm nhất “weren't vessels or windows. They were beads”. Bẫy: vessels và windows bị loại trừ; đáp án là beads.

items.text: Glassblowing made glass ___ enough for ordinary families
items.cue: glass became cheap enough for ordinary families
items.explain: Sau khi có kỹ thuật thổi thủy tinh, “glass became cheap enough for ordinary families”. Đáp án là cheap.

items.text: Venice, 1291: workshops moved to Murano because of the danger of ___
items.cue: the original reason was the risk of fire
items.explain: Bẫy: “Some people say this was to protect trade secrets”, nhưng “the original reason was the risk of fire” (risk = danger). Đáp án là fire, không phải trade secrets.

items.text: Green tint in cristallo removed by adding ___
items.cue: added small amounts of manganese
items.explain: Để loại bỏ màu xanh do sắt trong cát, “the Venetians added small amounts of manganese”. Đáp án là manganese; chú ý chính tả.

items.text: Glass is amorphous: atoms do not form a regular ___
items.cue: before they can form that pattern
items.explain: Khi nguội, nguyên tử bị “frozen in place before they can form that pattern”, tức “a regular, repeating pattern”. Đáp án là pattern.

items.text: Old windows thicker at the bottom because of how ___ installed them
items.cue: the glaziers who fitted them
items.explain: Bẫy: quan niệm thủy tinh là chất lỏng chảy chậm là sai; thật ra “the glaziers who fitted them usually put the thicker edge at the bottom” (fitted = installed). Đáp án là glaziers.

items.text: Float process: molten glass poured onto liquid ___
items.cue: a bath of liquid tin
items.explain: Trong quy trình float, “Molten glass is poured onto a bath of liquid tin”. Đề dùng gần nguyên văn, đáp án là tin.

vocab.vi: ổn định về mặt hóa học
quan niệm sai lầm phổ biến

listening.title: Reporting a lost bag at a station
listening.titleVi: Báo mất túi ở nhà ga
listening.context: A man visits the lost property office at a railway station to report a bag he left on a train.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a man reporting a lost bag at a railway station lost property office. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 7.

script.t: Good afternoon, lost property. How can I help?
Hi. I think I left my bag on a train yesterday, and I'm hoping someone's handed it in.
Oh dear. Well, nothing matching has come in today, but I'll fill in a report so we can contact you if it turns up.
Thanks, that would be great.
Were you travelling on one of our trains, or one run by another company? Some services that stop here keep their own lost property.
No, it was definitely one of yours. The commuter line.
Right, let's start with your name.
It's Oliver Fairclough.
Could you spell your surname for me?
Sure. F, A, I, R, C, L, O, U, G, H.
Thank you. And a contact number?
Lovely. And can I just check, you said yesterday? So that's the 11th?
Er, no, hang on. Today's the 13th, isn't it? So yesterday was the 12th. Sorry, I've lost track of the days.
No problem. The 12th of March, then. Which train were you on?
I normally get the quarter past seven into the city, but I overslept, so I caught the next one. That leaves at seven forty-five.
OK, that's the service from Millbrook, which arrives here at eight twenty.
That's right. I got off in a hurry and only noticed the bag was missing when I got to the office.
Now, can you describe the bag?
It's a backpack, a fairly big one, the kind you'd take hiking.
Do you know what make it is?
I'm afraid I can't remember. I've had it for about ten years and the label's worn off.
And what colour is it?
Most people would call it black, but actually it's dark green. It only looks black in poor light.
I'll put dark green. Is there anything unusual about it, something that would help us recognise it?
Yes, there's a little badge on the front pocket. It's shaped like a fox. My daughter gave it to me.
That's helpful. We get dozens of plain backpacks every week, so details like that really matter.
And what was inside the bag?
Well, luckily not my wallet or my phone. There's a water bottle and an umbrella, but those don't matter much.
The thing I really want back is my sketchbook. I'm an architect, and it's got months of drawings in it.
Oh, I can see why you're worried. I'll mark that as the main item.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 8 to 10.

script.t: So what happens now?
Bags left on trains are usually collected by the cleaning staff at the end of the line and sent back here within two days.
And when can I come and check? What are your opening hours?
We're open from eight until half past six on weekdays. On Saturdays we close earlier, at four, and we're shut on Sundays.
OK, I'll probably come on Saturday, then.
Fine. If you'd rather phone first, please quote your reference number. It's on this slip I'm giving you.
That way we can find your report straight away instead of searching by name.
Great. And is there any charge for getting it back?
There's a small handling fee. It used to be two pounds, but it went up in January, so it's now three pounds fifty.
That's fine, it's worth every penny if I get my drawings back.
Let's hope so. We'll text you as soon as anything comes in.
Thanks very much for your help.

groups.title: Lost Property Report
groups.instr: Complete the form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

items.cue: F, A, I, R, C, L, O, U, G, H
items.explain: Oliver đánh vần họ của mình: “F, A, I, R, C, L, O, U, G, H”. Chú ý chữ “C” ở giữa và cụm “GH” ở cuối, rất dễ bị bỏ sót khi viết.
Số điện thoại được đọc từng chữ số: “0, 7, 8, 4, 5 – 3, 1, 6, 0, 9, 2”. Cần nghe kỹ để không bỏ sót số 0 ở đầu và giữa dãy.

items.cue: So yesterday was the 12th
items.explain: Bẫy: nhân viên đoán “the 11th”, nhưng Oliver sửa lại “Today's the 13th… So yesterday was the 12th”, và nhân viên xác nhận “The 12th of March”.

items.cue: That leaves at seven forty-five
items.explain: Bẫy: Oliver thường đi chuyến “quarter past seven” (7:15) nhưng ngủ quên nên bắt chuyến sau, “That leaves at seven forty-five”. Còn “eight twenty” là giờ tàu đến, không phải giờ khởi hành.

items.cue: actually it's dark green
items.explain: Bẫy: “Most people would call it black”, nhưng anh nói rõ “actually it's dark green”, chỉ trông đen khi thiếu sáng; nhân viên ghi “I'll put dark green”.

items.text: Distinguishing feature: fox-shaped ___ on front pocket
items.cue: there's a little badge on the front pocket
items.explain: Đặc điểm nhận dạng: “there's a little badge on the front pocket. It's shaped like a fox”. Đề viết “fox-shaped ___” là cách diễn đạt lại của “shaped like a fox”.

items.cue: my sketchbook
items.explain: Bẫy: “water bottle” và “umbrella” có trong túi nhưng “don't matter much”; món anh thật sự muốn lấy lại là “my sketchbook”, được nhân viên ghi là “the main item”.

groups.title: Collecting the bag
groups.instr: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

items.cue: at four
items.explain: Bẫy: ngày thường mở cửa “from eight until half past six”, còn thứ Bảy “we close earlier, at four”; Chủ nhật thì đóng cửa.

items.cue: quote your reference number
items.explain: Khi gọi điện, cần “quote your reference number”; đề dùng “give” thay cho “quote”. Không phải tìm theo tên: “instead of searching by name”.

items.cue: it's now three pounds fifty
items.explain: Bẫy: phí trước đây là “two pounds”, nhưng đã tăng từ tháng Một nên “it's now three pounds fifty”, tức £3.50.

vocab.vi: nộp lại, giao nộp (đồ nhặt được)

listening.title: Welcome to Riverside Library
listening.titleVi: Giới thiệu thư viện công cộng mới
listening.context: A library manager gives a talk to local residents about the services and opening hours of a new public library.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a library manager talking to local residents about a new public library. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good evening, everyone, and thanks for coming. I'm Karen Doyle, and I'm the manager of the new Riverside Community Library.
We open to the public in three weeks, and tonight I'd like to give you an idea of what we'll offer.
There'll be time for questions at the end, so please hold on to them until then. And help yourselves to tea and biscuits at the back.
First, a bit of background. A lot of people assume the old library on King Street closed because the building was too small.
Actually, it had plenty of space. The real issue was that the roof had been leaking for years, and repairing it would've cost more than building a new library.
So the council decided to start again here, next to the river, which is also much closer to the bus interchange.
Now, opening hours. On weekdays we'll be open from nine in the morning until eight at night.
Originally we planned to close at six, but residents told us in the survey that they wanted to visit after work, so we've extended it.
On weekends we're open from ten until five, and that includes Sundays, which the old library never did.
Joining is free, as you'd expect. You can sign up online before we open, but you'll still need to come in once to collect your card.
And please bring something that shows your address, like a utility bill. We don't actually need photo ID.
Members can borrow up to fifteen items at a time. That's books, DVDs and audiobooks combined.
If you need longer, you can renew items online or with the app, as long as nobody else has reserved them.
Loans last three weeks, and there are no late fines for children's books, though adults will still pay a small amount.
Another thing I'm proud of is the building itself. It's not just about the solar panels on the roof, which lots of new buildings have.
What really makes it special is that the whole building was designed so that people in wheelchairs can reach every shelf without help.
Lastly, the café on the ground floor. It won't be run by the council. Instead, it's been handed over to a local social enterprise that trains young people for jobs in hospitality.

script.say: Now you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: Right, let me tell you about some of the special services we'll have.
Of course, there'll be the usual things, like free wi-fi, computers and printing. But we've added some new services that the old library simply didn't have room for.
On the first floor, there's a makerspace with two 3D printers. Anyone can use them, but because demand is high, you'll have to reserve a time slot in advance.
You can do that at the front desk or on our website.
Our staff will show you how to use them the first time, and after that you're free to work on your own projects.
Next to that is the recording studio, for podcasts or music. Some people expected it to be free, but there is a charge of five dollars an hour, to cover the equipment.
Then there's the homework club, which runs every weekday afternoon. It's aimed at primary school kids, so it's only open to children aged twelve and under.
Trained volunteers help with reading and maths, and parents are welcome to stay in the family area nearby.
We'll also have a language café, where people can practise speaking other languages over a coffee.
We know there are lots of families in the area who speak Vietnamese, Arabic, Italian and many other languages at home, so we think it'll be popular.
We're still finding volunteers to lead the groups, so that won't actually start until next month.
And finally, the seed library. You can take packets of vegetable and flower seeds home to plant, and you don't pay anything for them.
All we ask is that you bring back some seeds from your own garden at the end of the season, if you can.
OK, I think that covers everything. I'm happy to take any questions now.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: Why did the old library on King Street close?
options: The roof was too expensive to repair.
It was too far from public transport.
It was too small for the number of visitors.
items.cue: repairing it would
items.explain: Karen nói thư viện cũ “had plenty of space” (loại A); lý do thật là mái dột và “repairing it would've cost more than building a new library” (B). Gần bến xe buýt là ưu điểm của địa điểm mới, không phải lý do đóng cửa (loại C).

items.q: Why have the weekday opening hours been extended?
options: The old library had longer hours.
items.cue: they wanted to visit after work
items.explain: Ban đầu định đóng cửa lúc sáu giờ, nhưng “residents told us in the survey that they wanted to visit after work” – tức muốn đến vào buổi tối (A). Không nhắc đến kinh phí (B); thư viện cũ thậm chí không mở Chủ nhật (C sai).

items.q: What do new members need to bring to collect their card?
items.cue: something that shows your address
items.explain: Cần mang “something that shows your address, like a utility bill” = proof of address (C). Bẫy: “We don't actually need photo ID” loại A; đăng ký online chỉ là tùy chọn, vẫn phải đến lấy thẻ (loại B).

items.q: What does Karen say is special about the building?
options: It has a view of the river.
It is fully accessible to wheelchair users.
items.cue: people in wheelchairs can reach every shelf
items.explain: Pin mặt trời bị gạt đi: “lots of new buildings have” (loại B). Điều đặc biệt thật sự là “people in wheelchairs can reach every shelf without help” (A). Vị trí cạnh sông không được nêu là điểm đặc biệt của tòa nhà (C).

items.q: Who will run the café?
options: an organisation that trains young people
items.cue: trains young people for jobs in hospitality
items.explain: Bẫy: “It won't be run by the council” (loại A). Quán giao cho “a local social enterprise that trains young people for jobs in hospitality” (B). Tình nguyện viên được nhắc ở câu lạc bộ bài tập, không phải quán cà phê (C).

groups.instr: What does Karen say about each service? Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–G, next to questions 16–20.
options: C is for young children only
D starts at a later date
F is only open at weekends
G needs a staff member present

items.cue: reserve a time slot in advance
items.explain: Máy in 3D: “you'll have to reserve a time slot in advance” = must be booked ahead (A). Bẫy G: nhân viên chỉ hướng dẫn lần đầu, sau đó “you're free to work on your own projects”.

items.cue: there is a charge of five dollars an hour
items.explain: Phòng thu: “Some people expected it to be free, but there is a charge of five dollars an hour” → có thu phí (B). Bẫy: từ “free” xuất hiện nhưng bị phủ định.

items.cue: only open to children aged twelve and under
items.explain: Câu lạc bộ bài tập “only open to children aged twelve and under” = chỉ dành cho trẻ nhỏ (C). Bẫy F: câu lạc bộ chạy “every weekday afternoon”, không phải cuối tuần.

items.cue: won't actually start until next month
items.explain: Quán cà phê ngôn ngữ vẫn đang tìm tình nguyện viên nên “that won't actually start until next month” = bắt đầu muộn hơn (D).

items.cue: you don't pay anything for them
items.explain: Thư viện hạt giống: “you don't pay anything for them” = miễn phí (E). Việc mang hạt giống trả lại chỉ là lời đề nghị “if you can”, không phải điều kiện bắt buộc.

vocab.vi: ngành dịch vụ nhà hàng – khách sạn

listening.title: Planning a survey on social media for learning
listening.titleVi: Lên kế hoạch khảo sát về mạng xã hội trong học tập
listening.context: A tutor and two students discuss their plans for a survey about how students use social media for learning.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear a tutor and two students, Marcus and Priya, discussing a survey they are planning. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: OK, Marcus, Priya, come in. So, you're planning a survey on how students use social media for studying. How's it going?
Pretty well, I think. We've got a first draft of the questions.
We chose this topic partly because there's so much in the news about social media being a distraction.
But mainly because, when we talked to people on our course, almost everyone said they'd learned something from video clips or study groups online.
So we wanted to find out whether that experience is typical.
Good, that's a solid starting point. Who are you planning to survey?
At first we thought we'd survey the whole university, but we realised that would be impossible to manage in six weeks.
So we're going to focus on first-year students only. They're the ones most likely to be adjusting their study habits.
Sensible. And how will you actually reach them?
We'll still include all subjects, though, from engineering to history, so we can see if there are differences between them.
We considered handing out paper questionnaires in lectures, but that wastes a lot of paper and it's slow to analyse.
And posting a link on social media would only reach people who already use it a lot, which would bias the results.
So we'll send it through the student email system instead. Everyone has an account.
Good thinking about the bias. Now, what about your sample size? What are you aiming for?
We hoped for about five hundred replies, but from what we've read, response rates for email surveys are often below twenty per cent.
So we've lowered our target to two hundred. That still gives us enough to compare different subjects.
That's realistic. You could also send a reminder email a week later. That usually boosts the response rate quite a bit.
Good idea. We hadn't thought of that.

script.say: Now you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30.

script.t: Let me look at your draft. Hmm. It's a good start, but there are a couple of things I'd change.
First, it's far too long. Forty questions will put people off. You should cut it to around fifteen.
Yeah, we did wonder about that.
It's just that every time we discussed it, we thought of something else we wanted to know.
That always happens. But ask yourselves which questions really answer your research question, and drop the rest.
And second, some of your questions are leading. For example, 'How much has social media improved your grades?' assumes that it has.
You need to word those more neutrally. The layout and the font are fine, by the way, so don't waste time on those.
OK, that's useful. Should we offer a prize to encourage people to reply?
That's up to you, but it's not essential. Let's go through each section of the survey.
The first section asks about age, gender and subject. Where have you put it?
Right at the start.
People sometimes give up if the first thing they see is personal questions. I'd put that section at the end of the survey instead.
OK. Then the next section is about how often they use each platform.
At the moment you've got open questions there, and people will write all sorts of things. Use a scale, from never to several times a day.
That'll be much easier to analyse, too.
Should we list every platform, or just the main ones?
Just the main ones, with an 'other' box at the end. Otherwise the list gets endless.
The third section asks which learning activities they do, like watching tutorials or joining study groups.
This overlaps quite a bit with the section after it, on the benefits of social media. Why not merge the two?
Fair enough. Then the last section is about problems, like distraction and false information.
That part's really interesting, but some people may not want to admit to problems. Let them skip it if they want to.
So we'll make it optional.
Exactly. And before you send it out to everyone, try it with a handful of friends first to check that it all makes sense.
Will do. Thanks, Dr Hayes, that's been really helpful.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: What was the main reason the students chose this topic?
options: Their tutor suggested it to them.
Classmates said they had learned from social media.
There has been a lot of media coverage of it.
items.cue: almost everyone said they'd learned something
items.explain: Priya nói chọn đề tài “partly” vì tin tức về mạng xã hội gây xao nhãng (A chỉ là lý do phụ), “But mainly because… almost everyone said they'd learned something” từ mạng xã hội (C). Giảng viên không gợi ý đề tài (B).

items.q: Why have the students decided to survey only first-year students?
options: First-year students use social media most.
Other year groups have already been surveyed.
A larger survey would take too long.
items.cue: that would be impossible to manage in six weeks
items.explain: Khảo sát cả trường “would be impossible to manage in six weeks” = mất quá nhiều thời gian (A). Bẫy B: sinh viên năm nhất được chọn vì đang “adjusting their study habits”, không phải vì dùng mạng xã hội nhiều nhất; C không được nhắc.

items.q: Why will they not post the survey link on social media?
options: The results would not be representative.
It would be too slow to analyse.
It would use too much paper.
items.cue: which would bias the results
items.explain: Đăng link lên mạng xã hội “would only reach people who already use it a lot, which would bias the results” = kết quả không mang tính đại diện (B). Tốn giấy và chậm phân tích (A, C) là nhược điểm của phiếu giấy.

items.q: Why did the students reduce their target number of responses?
options: They expect few people to reply.
They want to compare different subjects.
They do not have time to analyse more.
items.cue: response rates for email surveys are often below twenty per cent
items.explain: Họ giảm mục tiêu từ 500 xuống 200 vì “response rates for email surveys are often below twenty per cent” = ít người trả lời (C). Bẫy A: “compare different subjects” chỉ là lý do 200 vẫn đủ, không phải lý do giảm.

groups.instr: Choose TWO letters, A–E.
groups.q: Which TWO changes to the draft does the tutor recommend?
options: A reducing the number of questions
groups.cue: You should cut it to around fifteen
groups.explain: Giảng viên khuyên cắt bớt câu hỏi: “You should cut it to around fifteen” (A), và sửa câu hỏi dẫn dắt: “word those more neutrally” (D). Bố cục và phông chữ “are fine” (loại B, E); giải thưởng “not essential” (loại C).

groups.instr: What do the students decide to do with each section of the survey? Choose FOUR answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–F, next to questions 27–30.
options: A move it to a different position
C change the type of answer
D combine it with another section

items.cue: I'd put that section at the end of the survey instead
items.explain: Phần thông tin cá nhân đang ở đầu, giảng viên khuyên “I'd put that section at the end of the survey instead” = chuyển sang vị trí khác (A), không phải bỏ đi.

items.cue: Use a scale, from never to several times a day
items.explain: Phần tần suất sử dụng đang dùng câu hỏi mở; giảng viên đề nghị “Use a scale, from never to several times a day” = đổi dạng câu trả lời (C). Bẫy F: chỉ thêm ô “other”, không thêm câu hỏi.

items.cue: Why not merge the two?
items.explain: Phần hoạt động học tập “overlaps quite a bit” với phần lợi ích, nên “Why not merge the two?” = gộp với phần khác (D).

items.cue: So we'll make it optional.
items.explain: Phần vấn đề có thể khiến người ta ngại thừa nhận, nên “Let them skip it” và Priya chốt “So we'll make it optional” (E). Phần này được giữ lại vì “really interesting”, không bị xóa (B).

listening.title: Coral reefs and ocean acidification
listening.titleVi: Rạn san hô và hiện tượng axit hóa đại dương
listening.context: A university lecture on how ocean acidification affects coral reefs.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture on coral reefs and ocean acidification. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning. Today we're looking at one of the less visible threats to coral reefs, and that's ocean acidification.
Let's begin with why reefs matter. They cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support around a quarter of all marine species.
They also have a very practical value for people living on the coast. A healthy reef acts as a natural barrier against waves, so it reduces erosion of the shoreline.
And of course, millions of people depend on reefs for food and for income from tourism.
Some reef organisms have even been used to develop new medicines, so there's a scientific value as well.
So, how is a reef built? A coral is actually a colony of tiny animals called polyps.
Each polyp produces a hard skeleton made of calcium carbonate, which it builds from minerals dissolved in the seawater.
Inside the polyps live microscopic algae. These algae provide the coral with most of its energy through photosynthesis.
They also give corals their colour. When corals are stressed, they push the algae out and turn white, which is what we call bleaching.
Bleaching is mostly caused by rising water temperatures, and you've probably seen the dramatic photographs. But acidification is a quieter problem, and in some ways a more worrying one.
Now to acidification itself. The ocean absorbs roughly a third of the carbon dioxide that humans release into the atmosphere.
That might sound like good news, but when carbon dioxide dissolves in seawater, it forms a weak acid.
Now, I should stress that the sea isn't actually becoming acidic in the everyday sense. It's still slightly alkaline. It's just moving in the acidic direction.
Since the industrial era began, the acidity of surface waters has increased by about thirty per cent.
Crucially, this process reduces the amount of carbonate available in the water. And carbonate is exactly what corals need to build their skeletons.
The result is that corals grow more slowly, and the skeletons they do build are weaker. You might expect them to be thinner, but in fact the main change is that they become more porous.
That makes the reef much more fragile, so it's more easily broken apart by storms.
There's a further problem. Some animals, such as certain sea urchins and worms, bore into coral and slowly break it down.
Experiments suggest that in more acidic water, this kind of erosion speeds up, so reefs may begin to shrink faster than they can grow.
Let me turn now to some research I find particularly encouraging. A team studying reefs off the coast of Palau in the Pacific found something unexpected.
The water in some of the bays there is naturally quite acidic, yet the corals were surviving well.
It seems these corals have adapted over many generations. Researchers now hope to identify the genes involved.
If they succeed, it might be possible to predict which reefs elsewhere are most likely to survive the coming decades.
This links to an approach called assisted evolution. Scientists breed corals that cope well with acidic conditions in a laboratory, and then transplant them onto damaged reefs.
It's still at an early stage, and it's expensive. Critics also point out that it can only be used on a small scale, not across an entire reef system.
So what can be done more broadly? Local action helps. Reducing water pollution from farms, for example, makes reefs more resilient.
Controlling overfishing matters too, because fish that graze on seaweed stop it from smothering young corals.
Some coastal communities are also restoring seagrass meadows near reefs. Seagrass absorbs carbon dioxide, which can lower acidity in the surrounding water.
But ultimately, none of these measures will be enough on their own. The only long-term solution is a large cut in global carbon emissions.
Next week, we'll look at how reefs are monitored using satellites and underwater drones.

groups.title: Coral reefs and ocean acidification
groups.instr: Complete the notes below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

items.text: Importance of reefs: protect coastlines by reducing ___
items.cue: it reduces erosion of the shoreline
items.explain: Rạn san hô là hàng rào tự nhiên chắn sóng: “it reduces erosion of the shoreline”. Đề dùng “protect coastlines” thay cho “barrier against waves… shoreline”.

items.text: Coral skeleton is made of calcium carbonate, built from ___ in seawater
items.cue: which it builds from minerals dissolved in the seawater
items.explain: Mỗi polyp tạo bộ xương canxi cacbonat “which it builds from minerals dissolved in the seawater”. Đáp án là “minerals”, không phải “carbonate” (đã có sẵn trong đề).

items.text: Algae inside the polyps supply most of the coral's ___
items.cue: most of its energy through photosynthesis
items.explain: Tảo “provide the coral with most of its energy through photosynthesis”; đề dùng “supply” thay cho “provide”. Bẫy: tảo cũng tạo màu (“colour”), nhưng câu hỏi nói về “most of”.

items.text: Ocean absorbs about a third of human CO2; seawater acidity up about 30% since the ___ era
items.cue: Since the industrial era began
items.explain: Độ axit tăng khoảng 30% “Since the industrial era began”. Cần điền tính từ “industrial” cho khớp với “the ___ era”.

items.text: Less carbonate in the water, so coral skeletons become more ___
items.cue: they become more porous
items.explain: Bẫy: “You might expect them to be thinner, but in fact the main change is that they become more porous” → đáp án là “porous”, không phải “thinner”.

items.text: Weakened reefs are easily damaged by ___
items.cue: broken apart by storms
items.explain: Rạn san hô trở nên mong manh nên “more easily broken apart by storms”; đề dùng “easily damaged” thay cho “broken apart”. Nhím biển, giun gây xói mòn là ý khác.

groups.title: Research and solutions
groups.instr: Complete the summary below. Write ONE WORD ONLY for each answer.

items.text: In bays off Palau, corals survive in acidic water, and scientists are trying to identify the ___ that help them adapt.
items.cue: identify the genes involved
items.explain: San hô ở Palau đã thích nghi qua nhiều thế hệ, và “Researchers now hope to identify the genes involved”. Đề diễn đạt lại “involved” thành “that help them adapt”.

items.text: In assisted evolution, tolerant corals are bred in a ___ and transplanted onto damaged reefs.
items.cue: in a laboratory
items.explain: Trong “assisted evolution”, các nhà khoa học “breed corals that cope well with acidic conditions in a laboratory” rồi cấy lên rạn bị hại; “tolerant” là cách nói lại của “cope well”.

items.text: Locally, restoring ___ meadows near reefs can reduce acidity, as these plants absorb carbon dioxide.
items.cue: restoring seagrass meadows near reefs
items.explain: “restoring seagrass meadows near reefs. Seagrass absorbs carbon dioxide”. Bẫy: “seaweed” (rong biển) cũng xuất hiện nhưng là thứ làm ngạt san hô non, không phải đáp án.

items.text: However, the only long-term solution is a major reduction in global carbon ___.
items.cue: a large cut in global carbon emissions
items.explain: “The only long-term solution is a large cut in global carbon emissions”; đề dùng “major reduction” thay cho “large cut”. Các biện pháp địa phương “none… will be enough on their own”.

listening.title: Booking a children's summer camp
listening.titleVi: Đăng ký trại hè cho trẻ em
listening.context: An American father phones a summer activity camp to book a place for his daughter.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a summer activity camp to book a place for his daughter. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 8.

script.t: Hello, Fernhill Summer Camps, Harriet speaking. How can I help you?
Hi there. I'd like to book a place for my daughter on one of your summer camps, if there's still space.
There certainly is for most weeks. Let me just open a booking form. Could I take your surname first?
Sure, it's Brennan. That's B, R, E, N, N, A, N.
Thank you, Mr Brennan. And your daughter's first name?
It's Lily. We only moved here from Ohio in the spring, so she doesn't know many kids yet.
Well, camp is a great way to make friends. How old is Lily?
She's eight right now, but her birthday's at the end of June.
We go by the age at the start of camp, so I'll put her down as nine.
Great, that's what I hoped. It means she'll be in the older group, right?
That's right, the nine to twelve group. Now, which week were you interested in?
I was thinking of the week beginning the 14th of July.
Hmm, I'm afraid the older group is completely full that week.
Oh, OK. In that case, could we do the week after? So starting the 21st.
Yes, the 21st is fine. There are still a few places left.
Each day the children choose a main activity for the mornings. We offer sports, art and drama.
She did a lot of soccer back home, but she says she wants to try something new.
She's been talking about being on stage for months, so let's go with drama.
Lovely. They put on a little show for parents on the Friday afternoon.
She'll love that. So what's the price for the week? Your brochure says a hundred and sixty-five pounds.
That's the full price. But if you book before the end of May, there's an early-booking rate.
So for you it would be a hundred and forty-five pounds for the whole week.
Excellent. Does that include lunch?
It includes a mid-morning snack and drinks, but the children need to bring a packed lunch each day.
No problem. And I should mention Lily has an allergy.
Thanks for telling me. Is it nuts? We're already a nut-free site.
No, people always assume that. It's actually kiwi. Even a small amount makes her really sick.
Right, I'll add that to her medical notes. Now, who will be picking her up at the end of the day?
Mostly her aunt, my sister-in-law. Her name is Grace Okafor.
Could you spell that surname?
Sure. O, K, A, F, O, R.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 9 and 10.

script.t: So, where do I take her on the first morning? Is it the main school building?
Most people think so, but the main building is being repainted this summer.
So we're using the sports hall instead. Just follow the signs from the car park.
Got it. Does she need any special clothes or equipment?
We provide all the costumes and materials. She won't need trainers or a swimsuit for drama.
But the only thing we insist on is a sun hat, because a lot of the games are outdoors.
OK, a hat. And how do I pay? Can I give you my card details now?
We don't take cards over the phone, I'm afraid, and we stopped accepting cheques last year.
I'll email you an invoice this afternoon, and you can pay by bank transfer from that.
Perfect. Thanks so much, Harriet.
You're welcome, Mr Brennan. We look forward to meeting Lily.

groups.title: Fernhill Summer Camps – Booking form
groups.instr: Complete the form below. Write ONE WORD AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

items.cue: B, R, E, N, N, A, N
items.explain: Ông bố đánh vần họ của mình: “Brennan. That's B, R, E, N, N, A, N.” Chú ý có hai chữ N ở giữa.

items.text: Child's age at start of camp: ___
items.cue: I'll put her down as nine
items.explain: Bẫy: Lily hiện “eight right now”, nhưng trại tính tuổi lúc bắt đầu trại nên nhân viên nói “I'll put her down as nine”. Đáp án là 9, không phải 8.

items.cue: the 21st is fine
items.explain: Ban đầu ông chọn tuần “the 14th of July” nhưng nhóm lớn đã kín (“completely full”), nên đổi sang tuần sau: “the 21st is fine”. Đáp án là 21, không phải 14.

items.cue: let's go with drama
items.explain: Có ba lựa chọn “sports, art and drama”; Lily từng chơi “soccer” nhưng muốn thử cái mới, nên ông chốt “let's go with drama”.

items.cue: a hundred and forty-five pounds
items.explain: Bẫy số: “a hundred and sixty-five pounds” là giá đầy đủ; giá đặt sớm (early-booking rate) là “a hundred and forty-five pounds”, nên đáp án là 145.

items.text: Food: child must bring a ___ lunch
items.cue: bring a packed lunch each day
items.explain: Bữa trưa không bao gồm, chỉ có “a mid-morning snack and drinks”; trẻ phải “bring a packed lunch each day”.

items.cue: It's actually kiwi.
items.explain: Bẫy: nhân viên đoán “Is it nuts?” nhưng ông bố phủ nhận và nói “It's actually kiwi.” Đáp án là kiwi.

items.cue: O, K, A, F, O, R
items.explain: Người đón là dì của Lily, “Grace Okafor”, và họ được đánh vần “O, K, A, F, O, R”.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: What must Lily bring to camp?
items.cue: is a sun hat
items.explain: Đồ bơi (A) và giày thể thao (B) bị loại: “She won't need trainers or a swimsuit for drama”. Thứ bắt buộc là “a sun hat” vì nhiều trò chơi ngoài trời.

items.q: How will Mr Brennan pay for the camp?
items.cue: pay by bank transfer
items.explain: Thẻ (B) bị loại vì “We don't take cards over the phone”, séc (C) cũng vậy vì “stopped accepting cheques”. Ông sẽ nhận hóa đơn qua email và “pay by bank transfer” nên đáp án là A.

listening.title: A town's new cycling scheme
listening.titleVi: Chương trình xe đạp mới của thị trấn
listening.context: A local radio presenter interviews a council officer about a new bike-hire scheme and cycling rules in the town of Marlow Vale.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a local radio programme about a new cycling scheme. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good morning and welcome back to Vale Talk. With me in the studio is Nadia Sheldon from the town council, who's here to tell us about the new cycling scheme.
Thanks for having me. Yes, from next Monday, Marlow Vale will have its own bike-hire scheme, plus a few new rules for everyone who cycles in town.
People often assume we've done this to cut pollution, and cleaner air will certainly be a bonus.
But the main thing driving it was the school run. Every morning, the roads around our three primary schools are completely jammed.
We want families to leave the car at home for those short journeys, which are often less than two kilometres.
And tourism? We do get a lot of visitors in the summer.
Visitors are very welcome to use the bikes, of course, but they weren't really the reason we set it up.
We ran a survey last year, and over half of parents said they'd cycle with their children if they felt the roads were safer and they didn't need to buy bikes.
So, how does it work? There are forty bikes spread across twelve docking stations around town.
Originally, we planned to give out plastic cards from the library to unlock them.
But in the end we decided that was too slow, so you simply download our app and scan the code on the handlebars.
The lock opens in a couple of seconds, and the app also shows you which stations have bikes available, and which have empty spaces for returning one.
What about people who don't have a smartphone? I imagine some older listeners will be asking that.
That's a fair point. The library staff will help anyone set up an account, and we're looking at other options for next year.
Now, as for charges. A lot of listeners have asked whether weekend use will be free. I'm afraid it won't.
What we're doing is making the first thirty minutes of every ride free of charge, at any time of the week.
After that, it's one pound for each additional half hour. Most trips in town take less than twenty minutes, so most people won't pay anything at all.
One thing I must stress: bikes have to be returned to a docking station, not left outside your house.
We won't suspend your account the first time. But if a bike is left anywhere else, you'll be charged a fine of fifteen pounds to cover collection.
And for teenagers, the scheme is open to anyone aged fourteen and over.
Fourteen and fifteen-year-olds don't need a separate permission form, but they must ride with an adult who also has an account.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: Let's talk about the new rules. I know some listeners are confused about where they can and can't ride.
Yes, so let me go through the main places. Starting with the High Street.
It's pedestrian-only during shopping hours, so cycling there is only allowed before ten in the morning, when the delivery vans come in.
Then there's the Riverside Path. It's very popular with walkers and dog owners.
We've kept it open to bikes, but there's now a speed limit of ten miles an hour, and wardens will be checking.
On Station Road, we didn't have room for a separate cycle lane.
So bikes will share the existing bus lane, and the drivers have all had extra training.
Abbey Gardens is a slightly different story. Cyclists can enter through the gates, which is handy as a short cut.
But once inside, you must get off and push your bike. It's a quiet space, and there are a lot of small children.
And finally, Quarry Lane, the steep hill up to the leisure centre.
It's fine for most of the year, but it gets icy and dangerous, so from November to February it's closed to cyclists completely.
All of these rules apply to everyone, by the way, whether you're on a hire bike or your own.
Maps showing every route and docking station are available free from the library and the tourist office, and on the council website.
That's really clear, Nadia. Thanks for joining us.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: What was the main reason for introducing the scheme?
items.cue: the main thing driving it was the school run
items.explain: Bẫy: ô nhiễm (A) chỉ là “a bonus”, còn khách du lịch (C) thì “weren't really the reason”. Lý do chính là “the main thing driving it was the school run”, tức giảm tắc đường quanh trường học (B).

items.q: How do users unlock a bike?
options: with a card from the library
by paying at the docking station
items.cue: you simply download our app
items.explain: Thẻ thư viện (B) chỉ là kế hoạch ban đầu (“Originally, we planned”) rồi bị bỏ vì quá chậm. Hiện nay “you simply download our app and scan the code”, nên đáp án là A.

items.q: What is free for all users?
options: the first hour of each ride
the first half hour of each ride
items.cue: the first thirty minutes of every ride free of charge
items.explain: Cuối tuần không miễn phí (“I'm afraid it won't”), nên A sai. Miễn phí là “the first thirty minutes of every ride”, tức nửa giờ đầu (C), không phải một giờ (B).

items.q: What happens if a bike is not returned to a docking station?
options: The user must pay a fine.
items.cue: you'll be charged a fine of fifteen pounds
items.explain: Tài khoản không bị khóa (“We won't suspend your account”), nên B sai. Nếu để xe sai chỗ, “you'll be charged a fine of fifteen pounds”, nên đáp án là A.

items.q: What is the rule for users aged 14 and 15?
options: They need a signed permission form.
They must be accompanied by an adult.
They can only ride at weekends.
items.cue: they must ride with an adult
items.explain: Bẫy: các em này “don't need a separate permission form” (A sai), nhưng “must ride with an adult who also has an account”. “Accompanied by an adult” là cách diễn đạt lại, nên đáp án là B.

groups.instr: What does the speaker say about cycling in each place? Choose FIVE answers from the box and write the correct letter, A–G, next to questions 16–20.
options: A cyclists must walk with their bikes
C cycling allowed only early in the day
D a new cycle lane has been built
F closed to cyclists for part of the year
G bikes can be parked overnight

items.cue: only allowed before ten in the morning
items.explain: High Street là phố đi bộ trong giờ mua sắm; xe đạp “only allowed before ten in the morning”, tương ứng C (chỉ được đạp xe vào đầu ngày).

items.cue: speed limit of ten miles an hour
items.explain: Riverside Path vẫn mở cho xe đạp, nhưng có “a speed limit of ten miles an hour”, tương ứng B.

items.cue: share the existing bus lane
items.explain: Bẫy D: “we didn't have room for a separate cycle lane”, nên không có làn xe đạp mới. Xe đạp sẽ “share the existing bus lane”, tương ứng E.

items.cue: you must get off and push your bike
items.explain: Được vào Abbey Gardens qua cổng, nhưng “you must get off and push your bike”, tức phải dắt bộ xe (A).

items.cue: from November to February it's closed to cyclists
items.explain: Quarry Lane bị đóng với xe đạp “from November to February”, tức một phần trong năm (F), không phải đóng cả năm.

listening.title: Tourism economics in small islands
listening.titleVi: Kinh tế du lịch ở các đảo nhỏ
listening.context: Two postgraduate students discuss their seminar presentation on tourism in small islands, then get feedback from their tutor.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two postgraduate students, Lachlan and Fiona, discussing their seminar presentation, and then talking to their tutor. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.t: So, Lachlan, we should decide how to open the presentation. I'd thought about starting with a map of all the islands.
Mm, everyone does that. I reckon we'd grab their attention more with a single case.
What about Tavira Cay, the island in that report? The one where tourism went from almost nothing to sixty per cent of income in ten years.
Hmm, or we could begin by defining the key terms. Some people in the group might not know what we mean by small island economies.
True, but definitions are a bit dry for the first minute. We can explain the terms once we've got them interested.
Good idea. Starting with one dramatic story makes the whole issue feel real. Let's do that.
Now, the bit I found most interesting when I was reading was the idea of leakage.
Where money spent by tourists flows straight back out of the island?
Exactly. I'd assumed the biggest cause would be foreign-owned hotels sending profits overseas.
But on most of the islands we looked at, the bigger loss was imported food. Hotels fly in almost everything their guests eat.
Yes, that surprised me too. Local farmers just can't supply enough, or not reliably.
Though I don't think it's that they refuse to sell to hotels. It's more that a small farm can't guarantee the same quantity every week.
Right. And the hotels can't risk running out of food when they're full.
What about the cruise ships section? I'm not sure how much to say.
Well, the passenger numbers look impressive, but they hardly spend anything on shore.
They eat and sleep on board, so the island gets the crowds without much of the income.
I did wonder about including the damage to coral reefs from the ships' anchors.
It's important, but it's really an environmental issue. Our focus is the economics, so I'd leave it out.
Right. So that's our point there. Cruise visitors bring congestion but very little spending.
And for the section on solutions, I think we should focus on the two policies that actually seem to work.
Agreed. We read about five, but some of them were never really tested.
The tourist tax on arrivals was one that clearly worked, because the money went straight into the water supply and roads.
And the other was linking hotels with local farms, so they buy produce from island growers. That cut imports quite a lot.
Limiting the number of visitors sounds good on paper, but no island has really tried it properly.
And luxury-only tourism and building a bigger airport both made things worse, if anything.

script.say: Now you will hear the students talking to their tutor. Look at questions 26 to 30.

script.t: Hello, you two. I've had a look at your slides. Shall I go through them section by section?
Yes, please, Dr Whitlock.
The opening case study is excellent. I'd keep that exactly as it is. It's vivid and well chosen.
The background section on island economies, though, is rather heavy. You've got four slides of history.
You could cut that down to one slide. The audience doesn't need that much.
Fair enough. What about the leakage part?
The argument is sound, but at the moment it's all words. A diagram showing where the money goes would make it much easier to follow.
And the cruise section?
That's my main concern. Your figures on passenger spending are from 2009.
You need more recent data there, or people will challenge you in the questions.
OK. And the solutions at the end?
Those are fine in content, but you've put them in as one long list. Try ranking them, from most effective to least.
Your audience will remember the top one or two far better than a list of five.
Should we finish with a recommendation for one particular island?
I wouldn't. Just summarise your main argument in a sentence or two, and leave plenty of time for discussion. The seminar group always has lots to say.
That's really useful. Thanks.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: How do the students decide to start their presentation?
options: with a definition of key terms
with the story of one island
with a map of the islands
items.cue: Starting with one dramatic story
items.explain: Bản đồ (A) bị chê vì “everyone does that”, còn định nghĩa (B) thì “a bit dry” và để giải thích sau. Hai bạn thống nhất “Starting with one dramatic story”, tức câu chuyện của một hòn đảo (C).

items.q: What surprised the students about leakage?
options: Foreign hotels kept most of the profits.
Local farmers refused to sell to hotels.
Imported food was the biggest cause.
items.cue: the bigger loss was imported food
items.explain: Lachlan tưởng nguyên nhân là khách sạn nước ngoài chuyển lợi nhuận đi (B), nhưng thực tế “the bigger loss was imported food”. Nông dân không từ chối bán (C sai): “I don't think it's that they refuse”.

items.q: What point will the students make about cruise ships?
options: Their passengers spend little on the islands.
They damage the local marine environment.
items.cue: they hardly spend anything on shore
items.explain: Hành khách tàu du lịch “hardly spend anything on shore”, nên đáp án là B. Ý về rạn san hô (C) bị loại vì “it's really an environmental issue... I'd leave it out”; còn A không được nhắc đến.

groups.instr: Choose TWO letters, A–E.
groups.q: Which TWO policies do the students say were successful?
options: B a tax on arriving tourists
D connecting hotels with local farms
groups.explain: Hai chính sách hiệu quả là thuế du khách (“The tourist tax on arrivals was one that clearly worked”, B) và liên kết khách sạn với nông trại (“linking hotels with local farms”, D). A thì “no island has really tried it properly”; C và E thì “made things worse”.

listening.title: How bees navigate and communicate
listening.titleVi: Cách loài ong định hướng và giao tiếp
listening.context: A lecturer in animal behaviour explains how honeybees find their way and share information about food.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how bees navigate and communicate. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning. Today we're looking at honeybees, and at two remarkable abilities: how they find their way around, and how they tell each other where food is.
A foraging bee may fly several kilometres from the hive, and yet it almost always returns directly home. So how does it do it?
The first and most important tool is the sun. Bees use its position in the sky as a kind of compass.
Of course, the sun moves during the day, and bees appear to have an internal clock that lets them adjust for that movement.
We know this from experiments in which hives were moved at night to unfamiliar places. The next morning, the bees still flew off in the correct compass direction.
But what happens when the sky is overcast? Even then, bees can still navigate.
That's because their eyes can detect patterns of polarised light, which pass through thin cloud and reveal where the sun must be.
Closer to home, bees rely more on what they can see. They memorise landmarks such as trees, hedges and buildings along the route.
In fact, young bees make a series of short orientation flights before they start foraging, circling the hive and learning the surrounding scenery.
If you move a familiar object, such as a tree in a pot, the returning bees can become noticeably confused.
And there's growing evidence for a fourth sense. Experiments suggest bees can respond to the Earth's magnetic field, although exactly how is still debated.
Let's turn now to communication. When a forager finds a good source of nectar, she returns to the hive and performs a dance on the honeycomb.
If the food is close by, she does what's called the round dance, simply circling one way and then the other.
Older textbooks say this is used for food within about a hundred metres.
But more recent studies put the figure lower, so the round dance seems to mean food within roughly fifty metres of the hive.
For food further away, the bee performs the famous waggle dance. She runs in a straight line, shaking her body from side to side.
The angle of that run tells the other bees the direction of the food in relation to the sun.
Remember that this happens in complete darkness inside the hive, on a vertical surface. So straight up on the comb stands for the direction of the sun.
If the run points, say, forty degrees to the right of vertical, the food lies forty degrees to the right of the sun.
And the duration of the waggle run indicates distance. The longer the run, the further they need to fly.
But the dance isn't the only message. The watching bees touch the dancer with their antennae, and pick up the scent of the flower she has visited.
That helps them to recognise the right flowers when they arrive.
The dance also carries information about quality. When the food source is especially rich, the dance lasts longer and is far more energetic.
So more bees are recruited to the best sites, without any single bee comparing all the options.
Bees can also send warnings. If a forager has been attacked at a feeding site, she may approach a dancer advertising that same site.
She butts it with her head and produces a brief vibration, which researchers call the stop signal. It reduces the number of bees sent to a dangerous place.
Interestingly, the same dance language is used in a quite different situation: when a colony splits and a swarm needs a new home, scout bees dance to advertise possible nest sites.
Finally, why does this matter beyond pure science? Bee populations are falling in many countries.
And one concern is that certain pesticides seem to interfere with navigation, so that bees simply fail to find their way back to the hive.
Understanding navigation in detail helps us test which chemicals are safe. We'll look at that research next week.

items.explain: Góc chạy cho biết hướng, còn độ dài cho biết khoảng cách: “the duration of the waggle run indicates distance”. Đừng nhầm với direction.

items.explain: Ong bị tấn công húc đầu vào ong múa và “produces a brief vibration”, được gọi là “the stop signal”.

items.cue: certain pesticides seem to interfere with navigation
items.explain: Mối lo là “certain pesticides seem to interfere with navigation”, khiến ong “fail to find their way back to the hive”.

listening.title: Hiring a van to move house
listening.titleVi: Thuê xe tải nhỏ để chuyển nhà
listening.context: A man phones a van hire company to arrange a van for moving house.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a van hire company to arrange a van for moving house. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good afternoon, Kestrel Van Hire, Gemma speaking. How can I help?
Oh, hi. I'm moving house soon, and I'd like to hire a van for the day, if that's possible.
Of course. I'll just take a few details first. Could I have your name, please?
Yeah, it's Josh Rendell.
Could you spell the surname for me?
Sure. It's R, E, N, D, E, L, L.
Lovely, thank you. And which day are you moving?
It's a Saturday, the 17th of March.
Oh, hang on, no – sorry. The 17th was the original plan, but the landlord changed it. It's the 24th now.
OK, Saturday the 24th of March. That's fine, we've still got plenty of vans that weekend.
Now, the driver needs a full licence. How long have you held yours?
Um, I think about five years. Actually, no, I passed my test just before I left uni, so it's six years.
Six years, great. We need at least two, so that's no problem. You'll just have to bring the licence with you when you collect.
And what's the best number to contact you on?
Thanks. Now, what size of van were you thinking of? We have small, medium and large.
I was going to go for a large one, to be safe. But it's only a one-bedroom flat.
Honestly, a large van would be far too big for a one-bed. And it's harder to park. I'd go for a medium one.
OK, you're the expert. Let's go with medium then.
Would you like any extra equipment? We supply moving blankets at no cost, so I'll put a few of those in the back anyway.
Great. I've got a washing machine, so could I hire a trolley as well? I don't fancy carrying it down two flights of stairs.
Yes, I'll add a trolley to the booking.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: So what's the total going to be? The website said fifty-nine pounds for the day.
That's the weekday rate, I'm afraid. At weekends the charge for a medium van is sixty-five pounds a day.
Ah, right. Fair enough. And is there a charge for mileage?
You get the first hundred miles free, and after that it's twenty pence a mile.
I'm only going about fifteen miles, so that won't matter, even with a couple of trips.
Now, insurance. Basic cover is included in the price, but if there's any damage, you'd pay the first nine hundred pounds.
Nine hundred? That sounds a lot.
It is. Most people take our extra cover. It's twelve pounds for the day, and it brings that amount down to two hundred and fifty pounds.
Yeah, I'll take that. I'm not used to driving anything bigger than a hatchback.
Very sensible. One last thing: fuel. The van comes with a full tank, and you need to bring it back with a full tank.
If you don't, we fill it up for you, but there's a service charge on top of the fuel, so it's much cheaper to do it yourself.
No worries, there's a petrol station right near you, isn't there?
That's right, just at the end of the road. So you can collect the van from eight o'clock on the Saturday morning.
Perfect. Thanks so much, Gemma.
You're welcome. I'll text you a confirmation now. Good luck with the move!

listening.title: A tour of a botanical garden
listening.titleVi: Tham quan vườn thực vật
listening.context: A guide welcomes visitors to a botanical garden and describes its zones and events.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a tour guide talking to visitors at a botanical garden. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good morning, everybody, and welcome to Larkspur Hill Botanic Garden. My name's Dana, and I'll be your guide for the next hour or so.
Before we set off, let me tell you a little about the garden's history, because it's not quite what most people expect.
Visitors often assume this was once the private grounds of a grand house. There is an old house at the top of the hill, but it was never connected to the garden.
In fact, the garden began in 1902 as a place where the state agricultural college grew and tested new crops. It only opened to the public in the 1950s.
These days we're a charity, and we rely on visitors like you, so thank you for coming.
We have more than eight thousand species here now, and around a third of them come from dry or mountain regions, which is quite unusual for a garden this size.
Now, a few things have changed this year. Some of you may remember the café being very crowded, but that was extended last summer.
And the sensory trail for kids has been here for several years now. What's brand new this season is a free audio guide.
You can download it to your phone using the code on your ticket, and it's available in six languages.
A quick word about rules. You're very welcome to bring a picnic, and in some areas you can even touch the plants – I'll tell you which ones.
But the one thing we really insist on is that you stay on the marked paths. Walking on the beds packs the soil down and damages the roots.
We also run a program of evening events through the summer. Entry to those isn't covered by your day ticket.
They often sell out, so you can't just turn up on the night. You'll need to reserve a place on our website beforehand.
Finally, the garden covers forty acres, and some of it is pretty steep. If anyone would rather not walk, we have an electric shuttle buggy.
It's free, but there are only six seats, so you have to book a seat at the main gate. It stops at every zone, not just the glasshouses.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: OK, let me give you a quick overview of the main zones, and what's happening in each of them this summer.
Our first stop will be the Desert House, the large glasshouse with the curved roof. It's full of cacti from Mexico and the southwestern states.
People ask if we hold a plant sale there. We used to, but now the plant sale happens at the visitor center.
What the Desert House does have is a night-time light display on Friday evenings, when the cacti are lit up in different colors. It's quite magical.
Next, the Herb Garden. This is one of the areas where you're allowed to touch and smell the plants.
And every Sunday at noon, one of our volunteers, who used to be a chef, gives cooking demonstrations using herbs picked from the beds.
Then we'll walk down to the Lake Meadow. It's the most popular place for picnics, and on Saturday afternoons there are open-air concerts there.
The meadow used to host our children's workshops as well, but those have moved indoors to the education center.
After the meadow, there's the Woodland Walk. It's beautifully quiet during the day, but if you're an early riser, it's at its best just after sunrise.
Once a month, our head gardener leads a guided walk at dawn there, listening for birdsong. You'll need to be here by five thirty, though!
And last but not least, the Rose Garden, which is at its peak right now. Lots of visitors bring cameras for that one.
It has over three hundred varieties, some of them bred right here by our own staff, and the scent on a warm evening is just wonderful.
In fact, we're running a photography competition there until the end of August. The winning picture goes on next year's ticket.
Entry forms are at the visitor center, and you can submit up to three photos each. The judges are looking for originality, not expensive equipment.
OK, if everyone's ready, let's head toward the Desert House. Watch your step on the way down.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

options: It was a site for testing new crops.
It was a public park for local people.

items.explain: Người ta hay nghĩ đây từng là “private grounds of a grand house” (A) nhưng hướng dẫn viên phủ nhận. Thực ra vườn là nơi trường nông nghiệp “grew and tested new crops”. Vườn chỉ mở cửa cho công chúng từ thập niên 1950 nên C sai.

items.cue: stay on the marked paths
items.explain: Được mang đồ ăn picnic nên B sai, và một số khu được chạm vào cây nên C sai. Điều bắt buộc là “stay on the marked paths” (= keep to the paths).

must be booked online in advance.
are included in the day ticket.

items.explain: Vé “isn't covered by your day ticket” (A sai) và “you can't just turn up on the night” (B sai). Phải “reserve a place on our website beforehand” (= booked online in advance).

items.q: What does the guide say about the shuttle buggy?
options: It costs a small amount to use.
It only goes to the glasshouses.
items.cue: you have to book a seat at the main gate

items.explain: Tại Herb Garden, một tình nguyện viên từng là đầu bếp “gives cooking demonstrations” (= cookery demonstrations) vào trưa Chủ nhật.

items.explain: “open-air concerts” = live music. Bẫy: các buổi workshop cho trẻ em (G) từng ở đây nhưng “have moved indoors to the education center”.

items.explain: Trưởng nhóm làm vườn “leads a guided walk at dawn there” – “at dawn” được diễn đạt lại thành “early morning”.

listening.title: Urban noise pollution
listening.titleVi: Ô nhiễm tiếng ồn đô thị – thảo luận bài tập
listening.context: Two students discuss their assignment on noise pollution in cities with their tutor.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two students, Hannah and Marcus, discussing their assignment on urban noise pollution with their tutor, Dr Whitcombe. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.

script.t: Come in, both of you. So, you're looking at noise pollution in the city. It wasn't on my list of suggested topics, was it?
No, it wasn't. And to be honest, we were worried there wouldn't be much research on it.
The real reason is that last term I was living above a bar, right on the main road. I hardly slept for three months.
So I got really interested in how noise affects people. Hannah agreed it would make a good project.
Well, first-hand experience can be a good starting point. Just make sure your personal feelings don't creep into the analysis. The report needs to be objective.
We've talked about that. We're keeping a separate log of where and when each recording was made, so everything can be checked.
Good. Now, you've been taking your own measurements. How did that go?
Mixed. We were worried we wouldn't be allowed into places like the railway station, but nobody stopped us.
And the weather was fine on all our recording days. The trouble was the app we used on our phones.
Yeah, we'd stand in exactly the same spot, and my phone would show sixty-eight decibels while Hannah's said seventy-four.
That's a common problem with phone microphones. The department has two proper sound meters you can borrow. I'd redo the key sites with those.
Oh, that'd be great. We'll do that next week.
What about the residents' survey? Let me see... the questions themselves look fine. They're clear and they're not leading.
My worry is that thirty-two responses isn't really enough to draw conclusions from. Can you get more?
We could put the survey on the community website. That should get us at least another hundred.
That would help, although people who choose to answer online may be the ones who are most annoyed by noise. Mention that as a limitation.
Good point. We'll add a note about that in the methodology section.
Good. And has anything in the results surprised you so far?
I expected traffic to be the main source of complaints, and it was, so no surprise there.
What I didn't expect was that the readings were higher on Saturdays and Sundays than during the working week. Probably because of the nightlife.
Interesting. That's worth highlighting in your discussion.
Now, you've listed quite a lot of health effects in your introduction. With three thousand words, you can't cover them all properly.
We know. Hearing loss is the obvious one, but city noise is rarely loud enough to cause that. It's more of a workplace issue.
And the evidence on blood pressure is quite technical. We decided to concentrate on disturbed sleep and on how noise affects children's ability to concentrate at school.
Good, there's plenty of research on both. I'd mention anxiety briefly too, but don't make it a main section.
OK. There's a study from a school near an airport that would be perfect for the section on children.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: Finally, the solutions section. Which measures are you evaluating?
First, noise barriers – those tall walls along motorways.
They work well, but each one costs millions. For narrow city streets, there's no way councils could afford them.
Agreed, the cost rules them out for most urban areas. What's next?
Quiet road surfaces. They're made of a special asphalt that absorbs sound.
And the council here has actually already laid them on two of the ring roads, so we can compare readings there.
That's a real advantage for your project. And planting trees along streets?
People love the idea, but the studies we found don't agree on how much difference trees really make. Nobody seems to have properly measured it.
So you'd say the evidence just isn't there yet. Fair enough. And the last one?
Banning lorry deliveries at night. From our data, that would make the biggest difference of all, especially to sleep.
Though shop owners might not be too pleased about it.
Perhaps not, but that's a question for your recommendations. Right, this is shaping up well. Send me a draft in two weeks.

groups.instr: Choose the correct letter, A, B or C.

items.q: Why did the students choose noise pollution as their topic?
options: They knew there was a lot of research available.
One of them had been affected by noise.
It was on a list of topics from their tutor.
items.cue: I hardly slept for three months
items.explain: Chủ đề “wasn't on my list” nên A sai, và họ lo “there wouldn't be much research” nên B sai. Lý do thật: Marcus sống trên một quán bar và “I hardly slept for three months”.

items.q: What problem did the students have when recording noise levels?
options: They were refused entry to some locations.
items.cue: my phone would show sixty-eight decibels while Hannah's said seventy-four
items.explain: Không ai ngăn họ vào nhà ga (“nobody stopped us”) và “the weather was fine”, nên B và C sai. Vấn đề: hai điện thoại đo khác nhau, “sixty-eight decibels while Hannah's said seventy-four”.

items.q: What is the tutor's opinion of the survey?
options: Too few people have completed it.
It should focus on traffic noise.
items.cue: thirty-two responses isn't really enough
items.explain: Gia sư nói câu hỏi “clear and they're not leading” nên A sai. Ông lo “thirty-two responses isn't really enough” (= too few people).

items.q: What surprised Hannah about the results?
options: Noise levels were higher at weekends.
Traffic caused fewer complaints than expected.
Residents worried more about night-time noise.
items.cue: higher on Saturdays and Sundays than during the working week
items.explain: Giao thông vẫn là nguồn bị phàn nàn nhiều nhất, “no surprise there” (A sai). Hannah bất ngờ vì mức ồn “higher on Saturdays and Sundays than during the working week” (= weekends).

groups.instr: Choose TWO letters, A–E.

listening.title: The psychology of habit formation
listening.titleVi: Tâm lý học về sự hình thành thói quen
listening.context: A lecturer gives a talk on how habits are formed and how they can be changed.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture on the psychology of habit formation. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning. Today we're turning to habits: what they are, how they form in the brain, and what psychology tells us about changing them.
Let's start with a definition. A habit is a behaviour that is triggered automatically, without conscious thought, by something in our surroundings.
How much of our lives do habits account for? Diary studies, in which participants record what they do each hour, give a fairly consistent answer.
Roughly forty per cent of daily actions are repeated almost every day, and usually in the same location. Place, it turns out, is a powerful trigger.
Psychologists often describe habits as a loop with three parts. First there's a cue, such as walking into the kitchen.
Then there's the routine – the behaviour itself, like switching on the kettle. And finally there's a reward, which is what makes the loop worth repeating.
Without the reward, the brain has no reason to store the sequence, and the behaviour simply doesn't become automatic.
Importantly, the reward doesn't need to be large. A small feeling of satisfaction, or a pleasant taste, is often enough to strengthen the connection.
So what's happening in the brain? Some of the clearest early evidence came from experiments in which rats learned to find chocolate in a maze.
At first, brain activity was high the whole time the rats were running. But as they learned the route, activity dropped sharply in the middle of the run.
It only rose at the start and at the end. In other words, once a behaviour becomes a habit, the brain can save energy by running it on autopilot.
That frees up our attention for other things, which is clearly useful – though, as we'll see, it also makes bad habits hard to shift.
Now, a question people always ask: how long does it take to form a habit? You may have heard the figure of twenty-one days. There's very little evidence for that.
In one study, volunteers chose a new daily behaviour and reported each day how automatic it felt. The average was over two months, but the range was enormous.
Simple behaviours, like drinking a glass of water after breakfast, became automatic within a few weeks.
More demanding ones, especially exercise, took far longer, and for some participants they never became fully automatic at all.
One encouraging finding was that missing a single day had almost no effect on the overall process. So the occasional lapse isn't a disaster.
What did matter was consistency over time. Participants who kept going after a missed day did just as well as those with a perfect record.
So how can we use this research? One useful technique is to attach a new behaviour to an existing habit.
For example, someone who wants to practise a language might decide to review ten words while their morning coffee is brewing. The old habit becomes the cue.
A second technique is to make the behaviour as easy as possible. Researchers call any small obstacle that makes an action harder friction.
Leaving your trainers by the door reduces friction for running. Even a delay of twenty seconds can be enough to stop a new habit forming.
What about breaking bad habits? Because habits are triggered by cues, the most effective approach is usually to change your environment.
This is why people often find it easier to give up smoking when they move house, or start a new job. The old cues simply aren't there.
Researchers have a name for this: the discontinuity effect. A major life change creates a short window in which new habits are easier to form.
Simply trying to suppress a habit, by contrast, rarely works. The cue is still present, and the urge often returns even more strongly.
Finally, a word about willpower. We tend to admire people who seem very disciplined, and assume they're constantly resisting temptation.
But studies suggest the opposite. People with high self-control actually face fewer temptations, because they've arranged their lives to avoid them.
In the seminar, we'll look at how these ideas are being used in public health campaigns.
