listening.title: Renting an allotment plot
listening.titleVi: Thuê một mảnh đất vườn cộng đồng
listening.context: A woman phones the local allotment society to rent a plot for growing vegetables.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning an allotment society to rent a plot of land for growing vegetables. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Hello, Millbrook Allotment Society, Clive speaking.
Hi, Clive. I saw your notice in the library. I'm interested in renting an allotment, if you've got any free.
We do have a couple at the moment, yes. Let me take some details and then I'll explain how it all works. What's your name?
It's Marta Delaney.
Is that D, E, L, A, N, E, Y?
That's right. Delaney.
And your address, Marta?
It's Flat 3, Rosewood Court. That's on the corner of Station Road.
Rosewood Court, lovely. And the postcode?
BR7 4QN. Thank you. Now, what size of plot were you hoping for? We have full plots and half plots.
Well, I was thinking of a full plot. I'd love to grow a bit of everything.
I'm afraid there's a waiting list of about two years for full plots. And to be honest, they're a lot of work for a beginner.
Two years? Oh dear. In that case, I'll take a half plot. That'll probably be more than enough to start with.
Very wise. We've got one half plot free right now. It's plot number thirty-two.
Oh, sorry, I'm reading the list upside down. Thirty-two was taken last week. The free one is plot twenty-three.
Twenty-three. And have you got any advice for someone just starting out?
Have you grown anything before?
Only on my balcony. I tried peppers once but they didn't do well. I've grown tomatoes for the last three summers, though.
Well, that's a good start. Tomatoes do very well up here.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: So how much is the rent?
A full plot is sixty-five pounds a year, and a half plot is thirty-eight pounds.
Is there any discount for students? I do a part-time course at the college.
Only for full-time students, I'm afraid. So it'd be the standard thirty-eight pounds.
Fine. And is there water on site?
There are taps by every path. But we turn the water off in November, because the pipes can freeze. It comes back on in March.
Makes sense. Are there any rules I should know about?
A few. Bonfires are allowed, but only after six in the evening. And you can keep bees, as long as you get permission from the committee first.
The one thing that isn't allowed at all is keeping chickens. We had problems with foxes a few years ago.
That's a shame, I quite fancied a few hens. Never mind.
And finally, before we give you a key to the gate, every new member has to attend an induction.
It only takes about an hour. I show you round, explain where the tools are kept, and so on. The next one's on Saturday morning.
Saturday's fine. I'll see you then. Thanks, Clive.

listening.title: Welcome talk at an outdoor centre
listening.titleVi: Buổi giới thiệu tại trung tâm hoạt động ngoài trời

script.say: Part 2. You will hear the manager of an outdoor activity centre talking to a group of new guests. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Evening, everyone, and welcome to Craigfell Outdoor Centre. I'm Callum, the manager. I hope the drive up the valley wasn't too bad.
First, a bit of background. Quite a few guests assume this building was once a hunting lodge, probably because of those old deer antlers in the hallway.
In fact, it was the village school until the nineteen seventies. The antlers were a gift from a local farmer when we opened.
Now, if you've stayed with us before, you'll notice one or two changes. The Wi-Fi is still only in the lounge, I'm afraid – the walls are just too thick.
And the drying room is where it's always been, next to the back door. But breakfast now starts at seven, half an hour earlier than last year, so you can get out on the hills sooner.
A few house rules. We'd rather you didn't wear walking boots upstairs, and please keep the noise down after ten.
But the one rule we never bend is this: before you go out walking on your own, you must fill in a route card at reception, saying where you're going and when you'll be back.
If you don't return on time, that card is what the rescue team will use to find you.
Packed lunches. They aren't included in the price – they're six pounds fifty each – and the kitchen needs to know by eight o'clock the night before.
There's a sheet on the kitchen door. Write your name on it the night before, and you can collect your lunch from the hatch in the morning.
And a word about the weather. The forecast goes up on the board every morning, and it's usually pretty good.
But up here, a sunny morning can turn into thick cloud in twenty minutes. Conditions change quickly, so always pack a waterproof, whatever the forecast says.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: Right, let me run through the activities you can sign up for this week.

Gorge walking is our most popular one. You climb up a mountain stream, through pools and small waterfalls. You don't need to be able to swim – the water's shallow and you're with a guide the whole time.
We provide wetsuits and helmets, but you will get soaked, so you'll need to bring spare clothes to change into afterwards.
Kayaking takes place on the lake. Sessions used to be in the morning only, but now they run all day.
For safety reasons, anyone kayaking must be able to swim fifty metres. We'll ask you to confirm that when you sign up.
Rock climbing is on the crags behind the centre. All the kit is supplied. The only problem is the rock gets very slippery, so if it rains heavily the session is cancelled.
Mountain biking. The trails are fantastic, but it's the one activity that isn't covered by your package. Bike hire is an extra fifteen pounds a day.
And finally, orienteering – finding your way round a course with a map and compass. It used to include an overnight camp, but we stopped that a couple of years ago.
You don't need any experience at all. It's ideal for complete beginners, and we'll teach you everything on the day.
OK, sign-up sheets are on the noticeboard. Dinner's at seven. Enjoy your stay!

listening.title: Observing museum visitors
listening.titleVi: Nghiên cứu hành vi khách tham quan bảo tàng
listening.context: Two students discuss their project on how visitors behave in a museum gallery with their tutor.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two students, Aisha and Ben, discussing their project on museum visitor behaviour with their tutor, Professor Hale. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 26.

script.t: Hi, Aisha, hi, Ben. So, your project is on how people behave in museums. Remind me why you picked the Maritime Museum.
Well, it's the closest museum to campus, which helped, but that wasn't really why.
No. They'd just redesigned their whole navigation gallery, and we thought it would be interesting to see how visitors used a brand-new space.
Good. And all the city museums are free, so that wouldn't have made a difference anyway. How did the observations go?
Mostly fine. It was never too crowded to follow people, and the lighting was good enough to take notes.
The difficulty was that some visitors realised we were watching them. One couple kept looking over at us, and then they started reading every single label.
That's a well-known problem in observation studies. People act differently when they know they're being observed. Mention it in your limitations.
Now, looking at your data, you've timed how long each visitor spent in the gallery. You've got a hundred and twenty people, which is a decent sample.
But you've mixed together people on their own and people in groups. Families with children behave very differently from someone visiting alone.
I'd keep the data for groups separate from the data for individuals. You don't need to collect any more, just re-sort what you have.
That makes sense. We did note down group size, so it won't take long.
Anything unexpected in the results?
We assumed people would spend most of their time at the big ship models, and they did. So that wasn't a surprise.
What I didn't expect was the touch screens. The museum spent a fortune on them, but most people walked straight past without touching them.
Interesting. Do you know why?
We think it's partly because they're placed on the wall behind the models, so people don't notice them.
OK. Now, you're also making recommendations to the museum. What have you decided?
We discussed making the labels larger, but actually the text is already a good size. So we dropped that.
What we will recommend is more seating. The average visit was only six minutes, and lots of older visitors left because there was nowhere to sit.
And shorter labels. Some of them are over two hundred words, and hardly anyone reads to the end. We'll suggest a limit of about fifty words.
What about an audio guide? Or reducing the number of objects?
An audio guide would cost far more than the museum's budget. And the curators were very clear that they won't remove any objects.
Then you're right to leave those out. Focus on what's realistic.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: Let's go through the sections of your draft report. The introduction?
We're both happy with it. I think that section's finished.
I agree, it reads well. Leave it as it is. And the literature review?
It's nearly two thousand words.
That's the issue. The content is fine, but it's too long for a report of this size. Cut it by about half.
Now, the methods section is rather thin. You need to add more detail – for example, how you chose which visitors to follow, and what times of day you observed.
OK, we'll expand that. And the results? We were thinking of adding photos of the gallery.
Photos might cause problems with visitors' privacy. What the results section really needs is a diagram – a floor plan showing where people stopped.
We can draw one from our notes. That should be easy.
Great. Send me the revised version by the end of the month.

listening.title: Mangrove forests
listening.titleVi: Rừng ngập mặn và vai trò bảo vệ bờ biển
listening.context: A lecturer in environmental science talks about mangrove forests, their value and how they can be restored.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture on mangrove forests. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at one of the most productive, and most threatened, ecosystems on the planet: mangrove forests.

Mangroves are trees and shrubs that grow along tropical and subtropical coastlines. They occupy what we call the intertidal zone – the strip of land that is covered by the sea at high tide and exposed at low tide.
Very few trees can survive there, because seawater is deadly to most plants. So how do mangroves manage it?
Some species have roots that filter out salt before the water even enters the plant. Others take in the seawater and then push excess salt out through their leaves.

The mud they grow in is another challenge. It contains almost no air, so many mangroves send up special roots that grow vertically out of the mud, like little pencils. These allow the tree to take in oxygen.
Reproduction is equally unusual. Instead of dropping seeds, mangroves produce seedlings called propagules, which start growing while still attached to the parent tree.
When they fall, they can float on the tide and stay alive for up to a year, which explains how mangroves have spread across whole oceans.
So why do mangroves matter? First, coastal protection. The dense tangle of roots acts as a natural barrier.
Studies have shown that a band of mangroves just a hundred metres wide can significantly reduce the height of waves, which protects villages behind them during storms.

Second, carbon storage. Now, you might expect most of the carbon to be held in the trunks and branches. In fact, the great majority is stored in the soil, where waterlogged conditions stop it from breaking down.
Hectare for hectare, mangroves can store several times more carbon than a typical rainforest.
Third, they support fisheries. The shallow, sheltered water among the roots provides a nursery for young fish, safe from larger predators.
Many of the fish caught offshore by local fishermen actually spent the first months of their lives in the mangroves.
Despite all this, the world has lost a large share of its mangroves in recent decades. Cutting trees for firewood plays a part, as does coastal building.
But by far the biggest cause has been the clearing of forests to create shrimp farms, which produce food mainly for export.
These farms often only last a few years before the ponds become polluted and are abandoned.
Which brings us to restoration. Many governments and charities have planted millions of mangrove seedlings. Unfortunately, a high proportion of these projects have failed.

The main reason is not a lack of funding, as people often assume. It's that seedlings were planted in the wrong location – on mudflats that are too low, where the young trees are underwater for too long each day.
The most successful projects take a different approach. They restore the natural flow of water first and let the forest regrow.
And crucially, they involve local communities from the start, because the people who live alongside the forest are the ones who will protect it in the long term.
Next week we'll look at seagrass meadows, which face many of the same pressures.

listening.titleVi: Đặt phòng tổ chức tiệc tại nhà hàng
listening.context: A man phones a restaurant to book a private function room for a party.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a restaurant to book a room for a party. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good morning, The Old Granary, Rosa speaking. How can I help?
Morning. I'm ringing about hiring one of your private rooms for a party.
Lovely. I'll just open a booking form. Can I take your name first?
Yes, it's Martin Okafor. That's O, K, A, F, O, R.
Thank you, Mr Okafor. And what sort of occasion is it?
It's for my mum, actually. Everyone thinks it's her birthday party, but it's really a retirement party. She's finishing work after thirty years as a nurse.
Oh, how lovely. I'll put it down as a retirement party, then. What date were you thinking of?
Friday the 8th of November. Oh, wait. No, my sister's away that weekend. It'll have to be the following Friday, the 15th.
Friday the 15th of November. Yes, that evening is free. How many guests are you expecting?
We sent out fifty invitations, but so far forty-two have said yes. I don't think we'll get any more replies now.
OK, forty-two. In that case, the Garden Room is too small – it only holds forty. So I'd suggest the Mill Room. It's on the first floor and has its own bar.
The Mill Room sounds perfect.
And what time would you like the room from?
I was going to say seven, but a lot of people are coming straight from work. Let's make it seven thirty.
Seven thirty. No problem.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: Now, food. We offer a cold buffet, a hot buffet, or a sit-down meal.
A sit-down meal feels a bit formal. And November evenings are chilly, so I think the hot buffet would be best.
Good choice. There are always vegetarian dishes in the buffet. Does anyone have other dietary needs?
My cousin's family are vegan. There are three of them, so we'll need three vegan meals.
Three vegan meals, I'll let the chef know. Now, to secure the booking we take a deposit.
The website says a hundred pounds, is that right?
That was the old price, I'm afraid. It went up in September. It's now 150 pounds, and it comes off your final bill.
OK, 150 pounds. Can we decorate the room? My sister wants to bring balloons.
Balloons are fine, and banners too, as long as you don't use tape on the walls. The only thing we can't allow is candles, because of the fire regulations.
Fair enough. I'll tell her. Thanks for your help, Rosa.
You're welcome. I'll email you the menu and an invoice for the deposit today.

listening.title: A community repair café
listening.titleVi: Quán cà phê sửa chữa đồ dùng của cộng đồng
listening.context: The organiser of a monthly repair café talks on local radio about how it works and who the volunteers are.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear the organiser of a community repair café talking on local radio. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

script.t: Hi, everyone. I'm Joy, and I run the Fixit Repair Café, which takes place on the first Saturday of every month in the church hall on Elm Street.
The idea is simple. Instead of throwing broken things away, you bring them to us, and one of our volunteers helps you repair them – for free.
We get asked a lot about what people can bring. Bicycles are very welcome, and so are clothes – we have two sewing machines.
Small pieces of furniture are fine too, like chairs and stools, as long as you can carry them in.
But there are two things we can't accept. One is microwaves. They can hold a dangerous electric charge even when they're unplugged, so it's just not safe.
The other is mobile phones. They need specialist tools and parts that we simply don't have. There's a phone repair shop on the high street that can help.
So how does a visit work? You don't need to book – just turn up any time between ten and two.
When you arrive, you'll be asked to sign a short form. It says that you understand we're volunteers, and that we can't guarantee every repair will work.
There's no fee. We do have a donations jar, but nobody is under any pressure to put money in it.
The other thing we ask is that you stay with your item while it's being repaired. We're not a shop where you leave things and come back later.
We want you to watch, ask questions and learn, so that next time you might be able to fix it yourself.
If you happen to have a spare part, then bring it along, but please don't go out and buy one specially. Our volunteers will tell you if you need anything.

script.say: Now look at questions 15 to 20.

script.t: Now let me introduce some of our wonderful volunteers, because they really are the heart of the café.
Derek has been with us from the very beginning. He used to look after the bikes, but these days he's our expert on clocks and watches. He's got incredibly steady hands.
Bikes are now handled by Phil, who's a keen cyclist. He can fix anything from a flat tyre to a broken chain.
Amira runs the sewing table. She'll mend torn jeans, replace zips and take up hems. She's also started teaching people to sew on buttons properly.
Sunita is a qualified electrician, so she deals with lamps, toasters, kettles and other small electrical items.
People often ask her to look at laptops as well, but none of us repairs computers – that really needs an IT specialist.
Gareth is a retired carpenter. His table is always covered in children's toys – wooden trains, dolls' houses, that kind of thing. The kids love watching him work.
And last but not least, there's Lucy. She trained as a jeweller, and she can repair broken necklaces, earrings and bracelets. She's become very popular.
So, come along next Saturday. And if you'd like to volunteer, we'd love to hear from you. Thanks for listening.

listening.title: Preparing a presentation on citizen science
listening.titleVi: Chuẩn bị bài thuyết trình về khoa học công dân
listening.context: Two students plan a seminar presentation about citizen science, in which members of the public help with scientific research.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two students, Sophie and Tom, preparing a presentation on citizen science. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.t: OK, Tom, shall we go through what we've each found out about citizen science?
Sure. The thing that really struck me was how long some projects have been going. One bird survey has been running every winter for over a hundred years.
I know, I saw that. For me the surprise was how accurate the volunteers' data is. I'd assumed amateurs would make loads of mistakes.
I wasn't that surprised by that, to be honest. Most projects have experts checking everything. And the number of people taking part, millions worldwide, is about what I'd expected.
Fair enough. What about the volunteers themselves? Why do you think they do it?
A lot of the surveys say it's about learning new skills, like identifying plants.

Maybe, but I'm not sure that's the main thing. Getting outdoors is nice too, but what people say most in the interviews I read is that they feel part of real science. Their observations end up in published research.
That's true. People like feeling their contribution counts.
Now, what about our example project, the one where people photograph ladybirds in their gardens?
Right. I thought the problem would be poor-quality photos, but most were perfectly usable.
And even when volunteers identified the species wrongly, the experts could correct it from the photo, so that wasn't a big issue.
No. The real problem was that most people sent in one or two photos and then never took part again. Keeping volunteers interested is the hard part.
So how should we show the growth in the number of participants? I made a map showing where everyone is.
The map looks great, but it doesn't show change over time. I think a line graph would show the growth much more clearly.
You're right. We could keep the map for later, when we talk about where the ladybirds were found. A table would be too hard to read on a slide anyway.
So what's next? Should we split the slides between us, or practise what we've got?
Neither yet. We still don't know the latest figures. First we need to email the project organiser and ask for them.
OK, I'll write to her tonight.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.t: We should also include some discussion points at the end. I've got a few opinions written down.
Go on.
Well, I really think volunteers should be told what happened to their data. They should get some feedback, even just a newsletter.
Absolutely. I feel exactly the same. Otherwise why would they keep going?
Second, I think the new smartphone apps have made it much easier for people to join in. You just take a picture and upload it.
I'm not convinced. Lots of older people, who are some of the most loyal volunteers, find the apps confusing. Paper forms worked fine.
OK, we'll present that as a disagreement.
Here's one of mine. Some big projects are basically getting expert-level work done for nothing. I think they're taking advantage of unpaid labour.
Hmm, I don't see it that way. Nobody's forced to take part, and they clearly enjoy it.
And what about schools? Kids could collect real data as part of their science lessons.
Yes, I'm completely with you on that. Schools should be much more involved. It would make science feel real to them.
Finally, I think all the results should be freely available to the public, since the public collected them.
It's not that simple, though. If you publish exactly where a rare species lives, people might go and disturb it. I'd keep some data private.
OK, that's another one we disagree on. That should make for a good discussion.

listening.title: The natural ice trade
listening.titleVi: Lịch sử ngành buôn bán băng tự nhiên
listening.context: A lecturer in economic history describes the rise and fall of the trade in natural ice in the nineteenth century.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture on the history of the natural ice trade. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning. Today we're looking at an industry that has almost completely disappeared: the trade in natural ice.
Before refrigeration, keeping food cold in summer was a real problem. And in the early nineteenth century, a few merchants in New England saw an opportunity.
Every winter, temperatures in the region fell far below freezing. The ice was cut from frozen ponds in large blocks, and the question was how to stop it melting before it could be sold.
The answer was insulation. Straw was tried first, but it rotted in damp conditions. The material that worked best was sawdust, which was cheap, because the region had many timber mills.
The first major attempt to sell ice abroad was a shipment to the Caribbean in 1806. The ice survived the voyage surprisingly well.
But commercially, it was a failure. When the ship arrived, there was no warehouse at the destination where the ice could be stored, so most of it melted on the dock.
The merchants learned from this. They built insulated ice houses in their main ports, and within a few decades ice was being shipped as far as India – a journey of four months.
As demand grew, so did the need for efficiency. Cutting ice by hand with saws was slow and dangerous work.

The key breakthrough was the invention of a horse-drawn plough, which cut deep grooves in the ice in a regular grid. The blocks were then all the same size, which made them much easier to stack and transport.
Ice was no longer a luxury. In cities, it was delivered to homes daily. But the largest customers were industrial.
The fishing industry used enormous quantities, but the biggest growth came from the brewing industry, because certain types of beer had to be kept cool for weeks while they matured.
Ice also transformed the meat trade. With the development of refrigerated railway cars, packed with ice and salt, meat could be sent across the country without spoiling.
So why did the trade decline? Machines that could make artificial ice existed from the middle of the century, but at first they were expensive and unreliable.

What really damaged natural ice was a problem of quality. As cities and factories grew, the rivers and lakes near them suffered from pollution, and people began to worry that the ice itself was unsafe.
Doctors warned against putting natural ice in drinks, and manufactured ice, made from clean water, started to look like the healthier choice.
A few unusually warm winters also caused shortages, which pushed prices up.
The final blow came in the early twentieth century, when electric refrigerators began to appear in ordinary homes. By the nineteen thirties, there was little need for ice deliveries at all.
In our next session, we'll compare this with other industries that were wiped out by new technology.

listening.title: Booking a river boat trip
listening.titleVi: Đặt chuyến du thuyền trên sông cho nhóm
listening.context: A woman phones a boat company to book a river trip for a walking club.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a boat company to book a river trip. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good afternoon, Kingfisher River Cruises, Neil speaking.
Hello. I'd like to book one of your river trips for a group, please.
Certainly. Let me get a booking form up. Could I have your name?
It's Hannah Lindqvist. That's L, I, N, D, Q, V, I, S, T.
Thank you, Ms Lindqvist. And is the group a company, or a school, or…?
No, we're a walking club. People often think we're a hiking society, but we're just called the Thornbury Walking Club. We fancied a day on the water instead of on our feet.
Sounds like a nice change. Which trip were you interested in? We have the short trip to Abbey Lock, or the full-day trip down to Carlow Bridge.
The full-day one, to Carlow Bridge. Some members wanted the short trip, but the full day includes lunch, so that's what we chose.
Lovely. And when would you like to go?
Saturday the 14th of June, if possible.
Let me see… I'm afraid the 14th is fully booked. But Sunday the 15th has space.
Sunday would be fine. Sunday the 15th, then.
Great. How many people will there be?
We have thirty members, but only twenty-six can come. Oh, and I should count myself – so twenty-seven altogether.
Twenty-seven. And the boat leaves from our pier at Westgate. Departure is at a quarter to ten, so please be there by half past nine.
A quarter to ten. Got it.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: Now, the price. The normal adult fare is twenty-two pounds, but groups of over twenty get a discount, so it's eighteen pounds per person.
Eighteen pounds each. That's good value. What's included in the lunch?
It's a picnic lunch served on board. Sandwiches, fruit and cake. If anyone needs a special diet, just let us know a week before.
One of our members can't eat gluten. Is that a problem?
Not at all. I'll note down one gluten-free lunch.
Thanks. And is there anywhere to leave bags? Some people may bring rucksacks.

There are lockers at the pier office, but on the boat there's limited space. What I'd really recommend everyone brings is a waterproof jacket. Even in June the weather on the river changes very quickly.
Good advice. And do we get a chance to get off anywhere?
Yes, the boat stops for an hour at Carlow Bridge. Most people visit the old mill there – it has a small museum, and entry is free with your ticket.
That sounds great. How do I pay?
We'll email you an invoice. Payment is due ten days before the trip.
Perfect. Thanks very much, Neil.

listening.title: A guided tour of a historic theatre
listening.titleVi: Tham quan nhà hát cổ có hướng dẫn viên
listening.context: A guide welcomes visitors to a restored Victorian theatre and explains the tour and the different parts of the building.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a guide talking to visitors at the start of a tour of a historic theatre. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14.

script.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Royal Lyceum Theatre. My name's Oliver, and I'll be your guide for the next hour or so.
The theatre first opened in 1872, and it was very nearly demolished in the nineteen sixties, when hardly anyone came to see plays here any more.
Luckily, a group of local actors started a campaign to save it, and after a long restoration it reopened twenty years ago.
Before we start, a few things. You're welcome to take photographs anywhere in the building, but please turn off the flash on your camera, because it can damage the old painted ceilings.

Some parts of the tour involve quite steep stairs. There is a lift to most floors, but not to the very top, so if stairs are difficult for you, please let me know and I'll show you an alternative route.
Bags can go in the cloakroom, which is free. You don't have to use it, but there isn't much room backstage.

Now, there are a couple of things you won't be able to do today. A lot of visitors hope to go up into the fly tower – that's the space above the stage where the scenery hangs. Sadly, that's closed for safety reasons.
And we won't be able to watch a rehearsal either. The company is rehearsing a new play at the moment, but the director has asked for no visitors.
What you will be able to do, though, is stand on the stage itself, and you'll get a chance to try on some of our costumes.

script.say: Now look at questions 15 to 20.

script.t: Let me tell you a little about the places we'll visit.
We'll start in the foyer, where we are now. Have a look at the floor – the tiles are all original, and they were made in Italy. They're the oldest thing in the building.

From here we'll go into the auditorium. People often expect the seats to be original too, but they were all replaced during the restoration. What's special about the auditorium is the sound. An actor can whisper on stage and you'll hear every word in the back row.
Then we'll climb up to the gallery. In Victorian times these were the cheapest seats, and people sat on wooden benches. Today it's where we keep a small exhibition about the history of the theatre.
After that we'll head backstage to the dressing rooms. These are being repainted at the moment, so you'll smell fresh paint, I'm afraid. They should be finished next month.
Next is the wardrobe department. This is where the costumes are made and repaired, and it's the busiest part of the theatre. Eight people work there full time.
And we'll finish in the café, which used to be the scenery store. It was only opened to the public last year, and it's already won an award for its design.
Right, if you'd like to follow me into the auditorium…

listening.title: A project on clothing waste
listening.titleVi: Dự án nghiên cứu rác thải quần áo
listening.context: Two students discuss their research project on what happens to unwanted clothes and how to reduce textile waste.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two students, Leah and Daniel, discussing their project on clothing waste. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.t: So, Daniel, how did you get on with the background reading?
Pretty well. The figure that shocked me was how little of our clothing is actually recycled into new clothes. Less than one per cent.
Really? I knew it was low, but not that low. What surprised me more was how quickly people get rid of things. Some items are worn fewer than ten times.
I'd read about that before, so it didn't surprise me so much. It was definitely the recycling figure for me.
OK. Now, for our survey of students, why did you think most people throw clothes away?
I assumed it would be because the clothes were damaged or worn out.
That's what I thought too, but actually, when I looked at the answers, most people said the clothes simply didn't fit any more. Fashion came second, and damage was way down the list.
Interesting. That's something we should highlight.
What about the charity shop visit? What did the manager say was their biggest problem?
I expected her to say they didn't have enough volunteers, but they're fine for staff. And they get plenty of donations – far too many, in fact.
So is that the problem?
Not exactly. The issue is that a lot of what people donate is such poor quality that it can't be sold. They have to pay to get rid of it.
Wow. So what should we do about the survey questions on shopping? Some of them seemed confusing.
I think we should just remove the questions about online shopping. There are too many of them, and they're not really our focus.
Hmm, I'd rather rewrite them, but you're right that they're off topic. OK, let's cut them.
And the deadline? Should we ask the tutor for more time?
I don't think we need to. If we finish the data analysis this week, we'll have two weeks left to write it up. That's plenty.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.t: Let's think about the solutions section. I've listed five ideas, and we need to say what we think of each one.
Go on, then.
First, clothes swap events, where students bring clothes they don't want and take something else home.
The ones on campus have been really popular. I think they're cheap to organise and we should definitely recommend them.
Agreed. Second, repair workshops, where people learn to mend their own clothes.
Good in theory, but they'd need trained people to run them, and the university says there's no money for that.
True. So that one's too expensive at the moment. Third, a tax on new clothing.
That's a government decision, though. It's not something a university can do anything about, so I'm not sure it belongs in our report.
Fair point. It's beyond our scope. Fourth, labels showing how long a garment is expected to last.
I like the idea, but nobody has measured whether labels actually change what people buy. We'd need more research before recommending it.
OK. And finally, rental services, where you hire clothes for special occasions.
Our survey showed students would use those for formal events like graduation. Several companies already offer it, so it could start straight away.
Great. So that's another one we can recommend.

listening.title: The history of lighthouses
listening.titleVi: Lịch sử và kỹ thuật xây dựng hải đăng
listening.context: A lecturer in maritime history describes how lighthouses developed, from early fires to automated modern lights.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture on the history of lighthouses. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good afternoon. Today I'm going to talk about lighthouses – how they developed, and why so few of them now have anyone living in them.

For most of history, sailors relied on simple fires lit on hills near the coast. The most famous early lighthouse, at Alexandria in Egypt, was built more than two thousand years ago, and it was probably the tallest building in the world for centuries.
Early lights burned wood, and later coal. Both had the same disadvantage: they produced a great deal of smoke, which often hid the light at exactly the moment it was needed.
Building lighthouses out at sea was a much harder problem. The first attempts on offshore rocks were made of timber, and several were simply washed away by storms.

The breakthrough came in the seventeen fifties, when an engineer designed a tower made of interlocking blocks of granite. Each block was cut to fit into its neighbours, so the whole tower behaved like a single piece of stone.
He also gave the tower a curved shape, based on the trunk of an oak tree, wide at the bottom and narrow at the top, so that waves lost their force as they hit it.
The next challenge was the light itself. Candles and oil lamps were weak, and much of their light was lost in every direction.

Mirrors helped a little, but the real advance came in the eighteen twenties with a new kind of lens, made of rings of glass, which bent the light into a single powerful beam. This could be seen from more than twenty miles away.
Of course, a ship's captain also needed to know which lighthouse he was looking at. So each light was given its own pattern of flashes, a kind of signature, which was printed on navigation charts.
In fog, light was of little use, so lighthouses were also fitted with horns, which could be heard when nothing could be seen.
Now, what about the people? Lighthouse keepers usually worked in teams of three, so that the light was watched all night.
The job was not so much dangerous as lonely. On offshore towers, keepers might spend two months at a time without seeing anyone except each other.
Their most important daily task was cleaning. Soot from the lamp built up on the lens and windows, and even a thin layer could reduce the light significantly.
During the twentieth century, electricity replaced oil, and then lights began to be controlled automatically. The last keepers in Britain left their posts in the late nineteen nineties.

Today, many lights are powered by the sun, using solar panels, and satellite navigation means ships depend on them less than ever. But they are still kept working as a backup if electronic systems fail.
Next week we'll look at the history of navigation charts.

listening.title: Booking a bike-repair workshop
listening.titleVi: Đăng ký buổi học tự sửa xe đạp
listening.context: A woman phones a cycle shop to book a place on a bicycle maintenance workshop.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a cycle shop to book a bike-repair workshop. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Hello, Spokes and Sprockets, Owen speaking.
Hi. I saw a poster about your bike-repair workshops and I'd like to book a place.
Great. Let me get the booking sheet up. What's your name, please?
Hannah Whitlock. That's W, H, I, T, L, O, C, K.
Thanks, Hannah. And a contact number?
Lovely. Now, we run two levels. The beginners' course covers the basics, and the advanced one is about gears and brakes in more detail. Which would suit you?
Well, I can already fix a puncture, but that's about it. I think I'd better start with the beginners' course.
Sensible. The beginners' sessions are on Tuesday evenings or Saturday mornings.
Tuesdays are difficult because I work late. So Saturday, please.
Saturday it is. The next one starts on the 12th of April, and it runs for four weeks.
And what type of bike should I bring? I've got an old mountain bike and a newer road bike.
Bring whichever one you ride most. You'll learn more on your own bike.
That's the road bike, then. I use it to get to work every day.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: How much does the course cost?
It's sixty pounds for the four weeks. But if you're a member of our cycling club, you get a discount, so it's only forty-five.
Oh, I joined the club last month, actually.
Then it's forty-five pounds for you. Now, we provide all the tools, but you'll need to bring a pair of gloves, because it gets quite oily.
Gloves, OK. Do I need anything else, like an apron?
No, we've got aprons. Just wear old clothes. And one more thing – the workshop isn't in the shop itself. It's in the unit behind the shop, next to the car park.
Behind the shop. Got it. Is there somewhere to leave the bike overnight between sessions?
Sorry, there isn't enough space. You'll need to take it home each week.
No problem. Thanks very much, Owen.

listening.title: Volunteering at a community radio station
listening.titleVi: Buổi phổ biến cho tình nguyện viên đài phát thanh cộng đồng
listening.context: The station manager of a community radio station gives a briefing to new volunteers.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a community radio station talking to new volunteers. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to Harbour FM. I'm Malcolm, the station manager, and I'm delighted to see so many new faces.
Let me start with a bit of background. Harbour FM began as a student project in a garage, broadcasting just two hours a week. Today we're on air eighteen hours a day.
We don't carry advertising for big companies. Most of our money comes from a grant from the town council, and the rest from local businesses who sponsor individual programmes.
All new volunteers do a training period before they go anywhere near a live microphone. That lasts six weeks, with one evening session a week.
Some of you have asked when you'll get your own show. To be honest, most people start by helping with an existing programme, usually as a producer, finding guests and checking facts.
Now, the most important rule in the building. Please never take drinks into the studio. Coffee on a mixing desk can do thousands of pounds of damage in a second.
Food is fine in the kitchen, of course, and mobile phones are allowed in the studio as long as they're switched to silent.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: Now let me show you around. Have a look at the floor plan on your sheet. We're standing in the reception area, by the main entrance.
Directly opposite reception is Studio One. That's our main live studio, and you'll recognise it by the red light over the door.
If you go down the corridor to the left of reception, the first door on your right is the music library. We still have about twenty thousand CDs and records in there.
At the end of that same corridor is Studio Two, which is smaller. It's used for recording interviews and adverts, not for live shows.
The newsroom is on the other side of reception, to the right, next to the stairs. That's where the news team writes the hourly bulletins.
Upstairs, right at the top of the stairs, is the training room, where you'll be spending your Tuesday evenings for the next six weeks.
And finally, the kitchen. It's the room between the newsroom and the fire exit. Feel free to make yourselves tea – just not in the studio!
Right, let's take a short break and then we'll begin.

listening.title: Evaluating a peer-mentoring scheme
listening.titleVi: Đánh giá chương trình sinh viên kèm cặp sinh viên
listening.context: Two students discuss their research project evaluating a scheme in which second-year students mentor first-year students.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two students, Priya and Lewis, discussing their project on a peer-mentoring scheme. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: So, Lewis, we've got all the questionnaires back now. Shall we talk about what we found?
Yes. I suppose the first thing is why first-years signed up for a mentor in the first place.
I expected it to be about academic writing, but very few mentioned that. And not many said they wanted help finding accommodation either.
No. By far the most common reason was that they felt lonely and wanted someone to talk to in their first few weeks.
Right. And what about how often pairs actually met? The university recommends once a week.
Hardly anyone managed that. Most met every two weeks, and a few only once a term.
Which brings us to the biggest problem the mentors reported. I thought it would be lack of training.
Some did say that, but the main complaint was that they couldn't find a time that suited both people. Their timetables just didn't match.
So how should we present our data on satisfaction? I was going to do a pie chart.
Pie charts are hard to compare. Since we asked the same question at the start and end of the year, I think a bar chart would show the difference best.
Good point. Let's go with that.

script.say: Now look at questions 25 and 26.

script.t: Now, what are we going to recommend to the student union? We should choose two main things.
I'd say paying the mentors, but the union said there's no budget, so that's not realistic.
Agreed. But matching mentors and students by subject seems really important. Students said a mentor on the same course was far more useful.
Definitely, that's one. And I'd like to recommend a proper training day for mentors before term begins.
Yes, let's include that. What about an app for booking meetings?
It sounds good, but the university already has a booking system that nobody uses. Another one won't help.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: Finally, our tutor asked us to comment on each part of the draft report.
OK. For the introduction, she said it was clear but far too long. We need to cut it to about half a page.
Right. And the literature review – she said we'd found good sources, but they were all quite old. We need to add some more recent studies.
For the methods section, I think the problem is that we haven't explained how we chose the students we interviewed.
Yes, she wrote that on the draft too. And the results section is fine, apart from the graphs. She said they need labels on the axes.
And the conclusion – she liked it, but said we should be more careful, because our sample was small. We can't claim our findings apply to every university.

options: A It needs more recent sources.

listening.title: The history of the printing press
listening.titleVi: Lịch sử máy in và cuộc cách mạng in ấn
listening.context: A lecturer in media history describes the invention of the printing press in Europe and its effects on society.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture on the history of the printing press. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good afternoon. Today I want to look at one of the most important inventions in the history of communication: the printing press.
Before printing, books in Europe were copied by hand, mostly by monks. A single Bible could take a skilled scribe more than a year to complete, so books were rare and very expensive.
Printing itself wasn't new. In China and Korea, people had been printing from carved wooden blocks for centuries, and Korean printers had even used metal type.
What Johannes Gutenberg achieved in Germany, around 1450, was to combine several existing technologies into one efficient system.
The press itself was adapted from a machine that was already common in the region: the wine press, which was used to squeeze grapes.
Gutenberg's real innovation, though, was a hand mould that allowed individual letters to be cast quickly and accurately from metal. Each letter was identical, and it could be used again and again.
He also needed a new kind of ink. The water-based inks used by scribes simply ran off metal type, so he developed an ink based on oil, similar to the paints used by artists.
The new technology spread remarkably fast. By 1500, there were printing presses in more than two hundred and fifty European towns.
Interestingly, the cost of the press was not the main expense for early printers. The greatest cost was paper, which could account for half the price of a book.
Many early printers actually went bankrupt, because they printed more copies than they could sell.

The effects on society were enormous. One was the standardisation of language. Before printing, the same word might be spelt in many different ways. Printers needed consistent spelling, and gradually the forms they chose became the norm.

Printing also changed science. Scholars in different countries could now work from identical copies of a text, including accurate diagrams, which had often been distorted when books were copied by hand.

Of course, not everyone welcomed the press. Political and religious authorities soon realised that printed ideas were difficult to control, and many introduced censorship, requiring printers to get permission before publishing.
And some scholars complained about the sheer number of books. They worried that readers would be overwhelmed by information – a concern that may sound familiar today.

Perhaps the most lasting effect, however, was on literacy. As books became cheaper, more ordinary people had a reason to learn to read, and reading slowly became a private activity rather than something done aloud in groups.
Next week, we'll move forward a few centuries and look at the arrival of the newspaper.

items.explain: Khuôn đúc cầm tay giúp đúc nhanh từng con chữ kim loại giống hệt nhau. Câu nghe được: “a hand mould that allowed individual letters to be cast quickly.”

readings.title: The Rise of Urban Farming
readings.summaryVi: Nông nghiệp đô thị đang phát triển ở nhiều thành phố, mang lại thực phẩm tươi và lợi ích xã hội nhưng vẫn gặp khó khăn về chi phí và đất đai.
readings.summaryEn: Urban farming is growing in many cities, bringing fresh food and social benefits, but it still struggles with costs and a lack of land.
readings.text:
For most of history, food was grown in the countryside and carried into towns. Today, however, a growing number of people are producing fruit and vegetables inside cities. This practice, known as urban farming, can take many forms, from small gardens on rooftops to large indoor farms in old warehouses.

One reason for its popularity is the wish to eat fresh, local food. When vegetables are grown close to where people live, they do not need to travel long distances by lorry or plane. Supporters argue that this can reduce pollution and help cities become more sustainable. In addition, food that is picked on the same day it is sold often tastes better and keeps more of its nutrients.

Urban farms also bring social benefits. In many neighbourhoods, community gardens give residents a place to meet, share skills and spend time outdoors. Teachers sometimes use school gardens to show children where their food comes from, and some studies suggest that young people who take part are more willing to try new vegetables. For older residents, gardening can be a gentle form of exercise.

Nevertheless, urban farming faces several challenges. Land in cities is expensive, so farmers may struggle to find suitable space. Indoor farms, which use artificial light instead of sunlight, can consume a great deal of electricity. As a result, the yield from these farms must be high enough to cover their costs. Soil in some urban areas may also contain harmful substances left by old factories, which means it has to be tested carefully before anything is planted.

Despite these problems, many experts believe that urban farming will continue to expand. It is unlikely to replace traditional agriculture completely, but it could become an important supplement, especially in crowded cities where fresh produce is hard to find.

questions.q: Urban farming only takes place on the roofs of buildings.
questions.explain: Bài nói nông nghiệp đô thị có nhiều dạng "from small gardens on rooftops to large indoor farms in old warehouses", không chỉ trên mái nhà → FALSE.

questions.q: Vegetables picked on the day they are sold may contain more nutrients.
questions.explain: Bài viết: food picked on the same day "often tastes better and keeps more of its nutrients" → TRUE.

questions.q: Most city governments provide free land for community gardens.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói đất đô thị đắt ("Land in cities is expensive"), không đề cập chính quyền cấp đất miễn phí → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why might soil in some urban areas need to be tested?
options: It may contain harmful substances from old factories.
It is too expensive to buy.
questions.explain: Bài viết: soil "may also contain harmful substances left by old factories".

questions.q: What do many experts think about the future of urban farming?
options: It will completely replace traditional agriculture.
It will soon disappear because of high costs.
It will grow and act as a supplement to traditional farming.
It will only be found in schools.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "unlikely to replace traditional agriculture completely, but it could become an important supplement".

readings.title: The Four-Day Working Week
readings.summaryVi: Tuần làm việc bốn ngày được thử nghiệm ở nhiều nơi; kết quả ban đầu khả quan về năng suất và sức khỏe, nhưng không phù hợp với mọi ngành.
readings.summaryEn: The four-day working week has been tested in many places; early results for productivity and well-being are promising, but it does not suit every industry.
readings.text:
The idea that people should work five days a week is so familiar that it is easy to forget it is a relatively recent invention. In the early twentieth century, many factory workers laboured for six days, and the two-day weekend was only gradually adopted. Today, a new proposal is attracting attention: reducing the standard week to four days without cutting pay.

Advocates of the four-day week claim that it can boost productivity rather than reduce it. Their reasoning is that employees who are well rested tend to concentrate better and waste less time. Trials carried out by companies and researchers in several countries have reported encouraging results, with many participating firms stating that output remained stable while staff reported lower levels of stress and burnout. Some organisations also found it easier to recruit and retain skilled workers, as the shorter week was seen as an attractive benefit.

However, critics point out that these trials have limitations. Most of the businesses involved volunteered to take part, which suggests they may have been particularly well suited to the change. In addition, the findings often rely on self-reported data, which can be influenced by participants' enthusiasm for the scheme. It is therefore difficult to know whether the same outcomes would be achieved across the wider economy.

Certain sectors face particular obstacles. Hospitals, schools and public transport, for example, must provide services every day, so a reduced week would require more staff or complex rotas. In such cases, the cost of implementation could be considerable. Small businesses with only a handful of employees may also struggle to cover absences.

For these reasons, many analysts expect a gradual and uneven shift rather than a sudden transformation. Some companies may adopt a full four-day week, while others experiment with flexible arrangements, such as compressed hours or reduced Friday shifts. Whatever form it takes, the debate reflects a broader question about how societies balance economic growth with wellbeing.

questions.q: The two-day weekend was introduced suddenly in the early twentieth century.
questions.explain: Bài viết nói cuối tuần hai ngày "was only gradually adopted" (được áp dụng dần dần), không phải đột ngột → FALSE.

questions.q: Some organisations in the trials found it easier to keep skilled staff.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Some organisations also found it easier to recruit and retain skilled workers" → TRUE.

questions.q: Employees in the trials were required to work longer hours on the remaining four days.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nhắc "compressed hours" như một lựa chọn trong tương lai, không nói người tham gia thử nghiệm phải làm thêm giờ → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why do critics doubt the trial results?
options: The trials lasted only a few days.
Participating companies volunteered and data were often self-reported.
Workers were paid less during the trials.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Most of the businesses involved volunteered" và "findings often rely on self-reported data".

questions.q: According to the passage, why might hospitals find a four-day week difficult?
questions.explain: Bài viết: hospitals, schools and public transport "must provide services every day".

readings.title: Microplastics in the Ocean
readings.summaryVi: Vi nhựa xuất hiện khắp đại dương từ nhiều nguồn khác nhau; tác động lâu dài còn chưa rõ và cần giải pháp từ gốc.
readings.summaryEn: Microplastics now appear throughout the oceans from many different sources; their long-term effects are still unclear, and solutions must tackle the problem at its source.
readings.text:
Plastic has transformed modern life, but its durability has created a serious environmental problem. Once plastic reaches the sea, it does not simply disappear. Instead, sunlight, waves and changes in temperature gradually break it into smaller and smaller fragments. Pieces less than five millimetres across are known as microplastics, and scientists now detect them in almost every marine environment they examine, from coastal waters to the deep ocean floor.

Microplastics come from a variety of sources. Some are the result of larger items, such as bottles and fishing nets, breaking down over time. Others are released directly in tiny form. Synthetic clothing, for instance, can shed fibres when it is washed, and these may pass through water treatment systems and eventually flow into rivers and seas. Vehicle tyres also wear away on roads, producing particles that are carried by rainwater into drainage systems.

The consequences for marine life are a cause of growing concern. Small animals such as plankton and shellfish can mistake microplastics for food. Researchers worry that the particles may accumulate as they move up the food chain, potentially affecting larger fish and, ultimately, humans who eat seafood. Laboratory studies suggest that some organisms grow more slowly when exposed to high concentrations, although it remains unclear whether similar effects occur in natural conditions.

Tackling the problem is complicated because microplastics are extremely difficult to remove once they are dispersed in the water. Cleaning the open ocean on a large scale is generally considered impractical. Consequently, many experts argue that prevention is more effective than cure. Proposed measures include improving waste management, designing washing machines with better filters, and encouraging manufacturers to use materials that degrade more safely.

Ultimately, the issue highlights the hidden costs of convenience. Reducing microplastic pollution will require cooperation between governments, industry and consumers, as well as further research into the long-term effects on ecosystems.

questions.q: Microplastics have been found in the deep ocean as well as in coastal waters.
questions.explain: Bài viết: scientists detect them "from coastal waters to the deep ocean floor" → TRUE.

questions.q: Water treatment systems remove all fibres released from synthetic clothing.
questions.explain: Bài viết nói sợi vải "may pass through water treatment systems" để ra sông biển, nên không bị loại bỏ hết → FALSE.

questions.q: Microplastics from tyres are more harmful than those from clothing.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ liệt kê lốp xe và quần áo là nguồn vi nhựa, không so sánh mức độ gây hại → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What does the passage say about laboratory studies?
options: They prove humans are harmed by seafood.
They show some organisms grow more slowly at high concentrations.
They found no effect on marine life.
They were carried out in the open ocean.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "some organisms grow more slowly when exposed to high concentrations".

questions.q: Why do many experts favour prevention?
options: Cleaning the open ocean on a large scale is impractical.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Cleaning the open ocean on a large scale is generally considered impractical. Consequently... prevention is more effective".

readings.title: How Sleep Affects Memory
readings.summaryVi: Giấc ngủ giúp não củng cố trí nhớ; thiếu ngủ làm giảm khả năng học tập, nên học sinh không nên thức khuya ôn bài.
readings.summaryEn: Sleep helps the brain consolidate memories; lack of sleep reduces the ability to learn, so students should not stay up late to revise.
readings.text:
Many students believe that staying up late to study is the best way to prepare for an exam. However, scientists who study the brain increasingly suggest that this habit may do more harm than good. Sleep, it seems, plays an essential role in helping us remember what we have learned.

When we learn something new, the information is first stored in a temporary form. During sleep, the brain appears to replay and organise these new memories, moving them into longer-term storage. This process is often called consolidation. Researchers believe that different stages of sleep may support different types of memory. For example, deep sleep may help us remember facts, while the dreaming stage may be linked to skills and creative thinking.

Experiments in several countries have compared people who slept after learning with people who stayed awake. In many of these studies, the participants who slept were better at recalling the information later. Some research also suggests that a short nap during the day can improve performance on simple memory tasks, although the benefits of napping may depend on its length and timing.

A lack of sleep, on the other hand, can make learning more difficult. People who are tired often find it hard to concentrate, and they may feel irritable or anxious. Over time, regular sleep deprivation has been associated with a range of health problems, which can further affect a person's ability to study and work effectively.

So what can learners do? Experts generally recommend keeping a regular routine, going to bed and waking up at similar times each day. They also advise avoiding bright screens late in the evening, as the light may make it harder to fall asleep. Rather than studying all night before an exam, students might achieve better results by reviewing their notes earlier and then getting a full night's rest.

questions.q: New information is first stored in the brain in a temporary form.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the information is first stored in a temporary form" → TRUE.

questions.q: Scientists agree that all naps improve memory, whatever their length.
questions.explain: Bài viết nói lợi ích của ngủ trưa "may depend on its length and timing", nên không phải mọi giấc ngủ trưa đều có ích → FALSE.

questions.q: Students who sleep well usually choose to study in the morning.
questions.explain: Bài không đề cập thời điểm học ưa thích của những người ngủ đủ giấc → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: According to the passage, which type of memory may deep sleep help?
questions.explain: Bài viết: "deep sleep may help us remember facts".

questions.q: Why do experts advise avoiding bright screens late in the evening?
options: The light may make it harder to fall asleep.
They reduce the time for studying.
They cause people to forget facts.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the light may make it harder to fall asleep".

readings.title: The Silent Loss of Languages
readings.summaryVi: Nhiều ngôn ngữ đang biến mất do áp lực kinh tế và xã hội; mất ngôn ngữ là mất tri thức văn hóa, và nỗ lực phục hồi cần cộng đồng chủ động tham gia.
readings.summaryEn: Many languages are disappearing under economic and social pressure; losing a language means losing cultural knowledge, and revival efforts need communities to take an active part.
readings.text:
Linguists broadly agree that a substantial proportion of the world's languages are at risk of disappearing within the coming generations. Unlike the extinction of a plant or animal species, however, the loss of a language rarely attracts headlines. It tends to occur quietly, as each successive generation uses the ancestral tongue a little less until, eventually, no fluent speakers remain.

The forces driving this decline are rarely a matter of deliberate prohibition alone, although historical policies of forced assimilation have certainly played a part in many regions. More commonly, the shift is propelled by economic and social pressures. Parents who perceive a dominant language as the key to education and employment may choose not to pass on their own, believing they are acting in their children's best interests. Urban migration, mass media and the internet can accelerate this process by exposing young people predominantly to a handful of global languages.

Why should such losses matter? One argument is that each language encodes a distinctive way of categorising experience. Vocabulary relating to local plants, weather patterns or kinship structures may embody knowledge accumulated over centuries, some of which is not documented anywhere else. When a language vanishes, this intangible heritage may disappear with it. Moreover, for many communities, language is inseparable from identity, and its erosion can be experienced as a profound cultural dislocation.

Efforts at revitalisation have produced mixed outcomes. Documentation projects, in which researchers record speakers and compile dictionaries, preserve valuable material but do not in themselves create new speakers. More ambitious initiatives, such as immersion schools where children are taught entirely in the endangered language, have reportedly achieved notable success in certain contexts. Nevertheless, such programmes demand sustained funding and, crucially, the commitment of the community itself.

The prevailing view among specialists is that external intervention can support, but never substitute for, local motivation. A language survives not because it is archived, but because people continue to choose to speak it in their daily lives.

questions.q: Language loss usually receives as much media attention as species extinction.
questions.explain: Bài viết: the loss of a language "rarely attracts headlines", trái với ý của câu → FALSE.

questions.q: Some parents stop passing on their language because they think it will help their children.
questions.explain: Bài viết: parents may choose not to pass on their own, "believing they are acting in their children's best interests" → TRUE.

questions.q: Immersion schools are cheaper to run than documentation projects.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói trường immersion "demand sustained funding", không so sánh chi phí với dự án ghi chép → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What is the main limitation of documentation projects, according to the passage?
options: They do not in themselves create new speakers.
questions.explain: Bài viết: documentation projects "preserve valuable material but do not in themselves create new speakers".

questions.q: What is the writer's main conclusion?
options: Archiving is the most effective way to save a language.
Global languages should be taught less in schools.
A language survives only if people keep choosing to use it.
questions.explain: Câu cuối: "A language survives not because it is archived, but because people continue to choose to speak it".

readings.title: The Growing Problem of Space Debris
readings.summaryVi: Rác vũ trụ quanh Trái Đất ngày càng nhiều, đe dọa vệ tinh và đòi hỏi cả giải pháp kỹ thuật lẫn hợp tác quốc tế.
readings.summaryEn: Space debris around the Earth keeps increasing, threatening satellites and calling for both technical solutions and international cooperation.
readings.text:
Since the first artificial satellite was launched in the late 1950s, the region of space surrounding the Earth has become increasingly congested. Alongside functioning spacecraft, it now contains a vast quantity of debris: defunct satellites, discarded rocket stages, and countless fragments produced by collisions and explosions. Because these objects travel at extremely high velocities, even a fragment no larger than a fingernail can inflict serious damage on an operational satellite.

Of particular concern is a scenario sometimes referred to as cascading collisions. The theory proposes that, once the density of debris in a given orbit exceeds a critical threshold, each collision would generate further fragments, which would in turn trigger additional collisions. In its most extreme form, this chain reaction could render certain orbits unusable for decades, jeopardising services on which modern societies have come to depend, including weather forecasting, navigation and global communications.

The rapid expansion of commercial activity has intensified these anxieties. Several companies are deploying large constellations of small satellites to provide internet access, and while operators generally design these craft to descend and burn up in the atmosphere at the end of their lifespan, the sheer number of launches inevitably raises the probability of accidents.

Engineers have proposed an array of mitigation strategies. Some focus on prevention, such as ensuring that satellites carry sufficient fuel to move themselves out of busy orbits once their missions conclude. Others concentrate on active removal, with concepts ranging from robotic arms and nets to harpoons capable of capturing derelict objects. Most of these techniques, however, remain at an experimental stage, and their cost is considerable relative to the size of the problem.

Perhaps the most formidable obstacle is not technical but political. Space is a shared environment, yet no single authority has the power to enforce rules across all nations and companies. Existing guidelines are largely voluntary, and compliance varies. Many analysts therefore contend that meaningful progress will depend on stronger international cooperation and a shared recognition that orbital space is a finite resource.

questions.q: Even very small fragments of debris can damage working satellites.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "even a fragment no larger than a fingernail can inflict serious damage on an operational satellite" → TRUE.

questions.q: Commercial satellite operators usually design their craft to remain in orbit permanently.
questions.explain: Bài viết: operators design craft "to descend and burn up in the atmosphere at the end of their lifespan" → FALSE.

questions.q: Harpoons have already been used successfully to remove large amounts of debris.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói các kỹ thuật như harpoon "remain at an experimental stage", không đề cập đã thành công trên quy mô lớn → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What does the theory of cascading collisions suggest?
options: Debris will soon fall back to Earth naturally.
Collisions could produce more fragments and further collisions.
Satellites will become cheaper to launch.
Only old satellites are at risk.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "each collision would generate further fragments, which would in turn trigger additional collisions".

questions.q: According to the writer, what is the greatest obstacle to solving the problem?
options: Political issues and the absence of a single authority
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the most formidable obstacle is not technical but political... no single authority has the power to enforce rules".

readings.title: The Psychology of Advertising to Children
readings.summaryVi: Trẻ em dễ bị quảng cáo tác động vì chưa hiểu hết mục đích thuyết phục; quảng cáo trực tuyến khiến việc quản lý khó hơn, cần cả luật lệ và giáo dục.
readings.summaryEn: Children are easily influenced by advertising because they do not fully understand its persuasive purpose; online advertising makes regulation harder, so both rules and education are needed.
readings.text:
Children have long been an important audience for advertisers. They not only spend their own pocket money but also influence many of the purchases made by their parents, from breakfast cereals to family holidays. This has led psychologists and policymakers to ask whether young people are able to understand advertising in the same way as adults.

Research into child development suggests that the answer depends largely on age. Very young children often struggle to distinguish between an advertisement and an ordinary programme. Even when they can tell the difference, they may not grasp that the purpose of an advert is to persuade them to buy something. This ability to recognise persuasive intent appears to develop gradually, and some researchers argue that it is not fully established until children are well into their school years.

Advertisers use a range of techniques that may be especially effective with young audiences. Bright colours, catchy songs and familiar cartoon characters can create positive emotional associations with a product. Free toys and collectable items encourage repeated purchases, while the use of celebrities or popular influencers may make a product appear desirable and fashionable.

The shift from television to digital media has made the issue more complex. Online, commercial content is frequently blended with entertainment, for example when a video creator promotes a product during an apparently casual review. Such content can be difficult even for adults to identify. Furthermore, digital platforms may collect data about users' interests and display targeted advertisements, raising additional concerns about privacy.

Governments have responded in different ways. Some have introduced restrictions on advertising certain foods during children's programmes, while others rely mainly on voluntary codes agreed by the industry. Critics argue that regulation has struggled to keep pace with new technology. Many educators therefore believe that alongside legal measures, schools should teach media literacy, helping children to question the messages they see and to make more informed choices as consumers.

questions.q: Children can affect what their parents buy.
questions.explain: Bài viết: children "influence many of the purchases made by their parents" → TRUE.

questions.q: Most children understand the persuasive purpose of advertising by the age of three.
questions.explain: Bài viết nói khả năng này phát triển dần và có thể chưa hoàn thiện "until children are well into their school years" → FALSE.

questions.q: Advertisements featuring cartoon characters are banned in some countries.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói một số nước hạn chế quảng cáo "certain foods", không đề cập cấm nhân vật hoạt hình → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why is online advertising particularly difficult to identify?
options: It is shown only late at night.
It is often mixed with entertainment content.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Online, commercial content is frequently blended with entertainment".

questions.q: What do many educators recommend?
options: Banning all advertising aimed at children
Teaching media literacy in schools alongside legal measures
Stopping children from using the internet
questions.explain: Bài viết: "alongside legal measures, schools should teach media literacy".

readings.title: Electric Vehicles and the Power Grid
readings.summaryVi: Xe điện tăng nhanh tạo áp lực lên lưới điện, nhưng sạc thông minh và công nghệ xe-về-lưới có thể biến xe điện thành nguồn hỗ trợ cho hệ thống.
readings.summaryEn: The rapid growth of electric cars puts pressure on the power grid, but smart charging and vehicle-to-grid technology could turn them into a support for the system.
readings.text:
As governments seek to cut carbon emissions from transport, electric vehicles are becoming an increasingly common sight on the roads. This transition, however, raises an important question: can existing electricity networks cope with millions of cars that need to be charged every day?

The challenge is not simply the total amount of electricity required. In many places, energy analysts suggest that overall generation capacity could expand to meet the additional demand over time. The more pressing issue is timing. If large numbers of drivers return home in the early evening and plug in their cars at the same moment, they could create a sharp peak in demand, coinciding with the period when households are already cooking, heating and using appliances. Local distribution networks, particularly in older residential areas, may not have been designed to handle such loads.

One promising solution is smart charging. Instead of drawing power immediately, a smart charger can delay charging until demand is lower, such as late at night, or adjust its rate according to signals from the grid operator. Drivers may be offered cheaper tariffs in exchange for allowing this flexibility. Since most cars remain parked for many hours, the delay is usually inconvenient for only a small number of users.

A more ambitious idea is known as vehicle-to-grid technology. In this system, the batteries of parked electric cars could not only receive electricity but also return it to the network when needed. Collectively, these vehicles could act as a large, distributed storage system, helping to balance supply from renewable sources such as wind and solar power, which fluctuate with the weather. Pilot projects have explored the concept, although concerns remain about battery wear and the complexity of coordinating thousands of vehicles.

In summary, electric vehicles present both a challenge and an opportunity for power systems. With careful planning, investment in infrastructure and appropriate incentives, they could become a valuable asset rather than a burden.

questions.q: The writer believes the main problem is the timing of charging rather than total demand.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "The challenge is not simply the total amount... The more pressing issue is timing." → TRUE.

questions.q: Smart charging always charges a car immediately when it is plugged in.
questions.explain: Bài viết: smart charger "can delay charging until demand is lower", ngược với "immediately" → FALSE.

questions.q: Vehicle-to-grid technology is already used in most countries.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói có "pilot projects" thử nghiệm, không nói về mức độ phổ biến ở các nước → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why might older residential areas face difficulties?
options: They have no access to renewable energy.
Their local networks may not be designed for such loads.
Residents there do not own cars.
questions.explain: Bài viết: local networks in older residential areas "may not have been designed to handle such loads".

questions.q: What concern about vehicle-to-grid technology is mentioned?
questions.explain: Bài viết: "concerns remain about battery wear and the complexity of coordinating thousands of vehicles".

readings.title: Museums in the Digital Age
