readings.summaryVi: Bảo tàng dùng công nghệ số để mở rộng tiếp cận, nhưng trải nghiệm xem hiện vật thật vẫn có giá trị riêng.
readings.summaryEn: Museums use digital technology to reach more people, but seeing real objects in person still has a value of its own.
readings.text:
Museums have traditionally been quiet places where visitors walk slowly past glass cases and read small labels. In recent years, however, technology has started to change the way people experience art, history and science. Many museums now offer a wide range of digital services, both inside their buildings and online.

One major development is the online collection. By photographing objects and putting the images on their websites, museums allow people to explore their collections from anywhere in the world. This is especially useful for students, researchers and people who live far away or cannot travel. Some institutions also create virtual tours, which let users move through the galleries on a computer or phone as if they were really there.

Inside museums, technology can make exhibitions more interactive. Touch screens, audio guides and smartphone apps provide extra information about each object. Some exhibitions use augmented reality, where a phone or headset adds digital images to the real world. A visitor might, for example, see an ancient building appear in its original colours. Museum staff often say that these tools are popular with younger visitors, who are used to learning through screens.

Not everyone is convinced, though. Some critics worry that too much technology can distract visitors from the objects themselves. Instead of looking closely at a painting, people may spend their time staring at their phones. There are also practical concerns: digital equipment can be expensive to buy and maintain, and smaller museums may not have enough money or staff to keep it working.

Most experts agree that technology should support, not replace, the traditional museum visit. Seeing a real object, with its true size, texture and age, can be a powerful experience that a screen cannot fully reproduce. The challenge for museums is to find the right balance between the physical and the digital, so that they remain relevant to new generations.

questions.q: Online collections help people who live far from a museum.
questions.explain: Bài viết: online collections are "especially useful for... people who live far away or cannot travel" → TRUE.

questions.q: Museum staff say that digital tools are unpopular with younger visitors.
questions.explain: Bài viết: staff say these tools "are popular with younger visitors" → FALSE.

questions.q: Virtual tours attract more visitors than real museum visits.
questions.explain: Bài không so sánh số lượng người dùng tour ảo với khách tham quan trực tiếp → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What is one practical concern about digital equipment?
options: It is expensive to buy and maintain.
It is too difficult for children.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "digital equipment can be expensive to buy and maintain".

questions.q: What do most experts believe about technology in museums?
options: It should be removed from galleries.
It should support, not replace, the traditional visit.
It is only useful for researchers.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "technology should support, not replace, the traditional museum visit".

readings.title: Ageing Populations and Healthcare
readings.summaryVi: Dân số già hóa gây áp lực lên hệ thống y tế; các giải pháp gồm phòng bệnh, chăm sóc tại cộng đồng và công nghệ, nhưng đều có hạn chế.
readings.summaryEn: An ageing population puts pressure on health systems; solutions include prevention, community care and technology, but each has its limits.
readings.text:
Across much of the world, populations are growing older. Rising life expectancy, combined with declining birth rates, means that the proportion of people over the age of sixty-five is increasing steadily in many countries. While this demographic shift is in many respects a testament to advances in medicine and living standards, it also poses profound challenges for healthcare systems that were largely designed around the treatment of acute, short-term illness.

Older adults are more likely to live with chronic conditions, such as heart disease, diabetes and arthritis, and many experience several of these simultaneously. Managing multiple long-term conditions tends to be both complex and costly, requiring ongoing monitoring, numerous medications and coordination between different specialists. Consequently, health economists frequently warn that expenditure may rise faster than the revenue available to fund it, particularly where a shrinking working-age population contributes a smaller share of taxes.

In response, many policymakers advocate a reorientation towards prevention. Encouraging physical activity, balanced nutrition and social engagement throughout life may postpone the onset of disability and reduce dependence on hospital services. Equally, there is growing interest in delivering care within the community rather than in hospitals. Home visits, local clinics and support for family carers are often regarded as more humane and potentially less expensive, although their effectiveness depends heavily on adequate staffing and funding.

Technology is frequently presented as part of the solution. Remote monitoring devices, for instance, can alert medical teams to changes in a patient's condition, while telemedicine allows consultations without the need to travel. Nevertheless, such innovations are not a panacea. Some older people lack the confidence or resources to use digital tools, and there is a risk that technology could exacerbate isolation if it replaces, rather than complements, human contact.

Ultimately, adapting to an ageing society will require more than incremental adjustments. It calls for a fundamental rethinking of how care is organised, financed and delivered, so that longer lives can also be healthier and more fulfilling ones.

questions.q: Many current healthcare systems were mainly designed to treat short-term illness.
questions.explain: Bài viết: systems "were largely designed around the treatment of acute, short-term illness" → TRUE.

questions.q: Community-based care is always cheaper than hospital treatment.
questions.explain: Bài viết chỉ nói "potentially less expensive" và hiệu quả phụ thuộc vào nhân lực, kinh phí, nên không phải "always" → FALSE.

questions.q: Most older people prefer telemedicine to face-to-face appointments.
questions.explain: Bài không đề cập sở thích của người cao tuổi giữa khám từ xa và khám trực tiếp → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why might healthcare spending become difficult to fund?
options: A smaller working-age population contributes a smaller share of taxes.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "a shrinking working-age population contributes a smaller share of taxes".

questions.q: What risk of technology does the writer mention?
options: It may increase isolation if it replaces human contact.
It is too slow to detect changes.
It requires patients to travel more.
It is banned in some hospitals.
questions.explain: Bài viết: technology "could exacerbate isolation if it replaces, rather than complements, human contact".

readings.title: Why We Throw Away So Much Food
readings.summaryVi: Khoảng một phần ba lượng thực phẩm trên thế giới bị bỏ phí; bài viết giải thích nguyên nhân, tác hại với môi trường và những thói quen nhỏ giúp giảm lãng phí.
readings.summaryEn: About a third of the world's food is wasted; the article explains the causes, the harm to the environment and the small habits that help reduce waste.
readings.text:
Every year, people around the world throw away a huge amount of food. Experts say that about one third of all the food we produce is never eaten. Some of it is lost on farms or during transport, but a large part is wasted in our own homes.

Why does this happen? One common reason is that people buy too much. When food is on special offer in the supermarket, it is easy to fill the basket with more than we need. Another reason is confusion about the dates on packets. Many people think that food must go in the bin after its "best before" date, but this date is only about quality, not safety. Food is often still good to eat after it.

Food waste is also a problem for the environment. When old food goes to a landfill, it slowly breaks down and produces gases that make the planet warmer. In addition, a lot of water, energy and land was used to grow the food in the first place, so all of these resources are wasted too.

The good news is that small changes can help. Before going shopping, you can check your fridge and write a list. You can keep leftovers in a box and eat them the next day. Some families freeze bread and fruit so that they last longer. In several countries, there are now apps that let shops and cafés sell unsold meals cheaply at the end of the day.

If everyone wasted a little less, the total amount would fall a lot. And there is one more reason to try: saving food also means saving money.

questions.q: About one third of the food produced in the world is never eaten.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "about one third of all the food we produce is never eaten" → TRUE.

questions.q: The "best before" date tells you when food becomes dangerous to eat.
questions.explain: Bài viết nói ngày "best before" chỉ liên quan đến chất lượng: "this date is only about quality, not safety" → FALSE.

questions.q: Supermarkets in most countries give unsold food to poor families.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nhắc đến ứng dụng giúp cửa hàng bán rẻ đồ ăn còn thừa, không nói siêu thị tặng thực phẩm cho gia đình nghèo → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: According to the text, why do people often buy too much food?
options: They do not have a fridge.
They use apps to do their shopping.
Food is on special offer in the supermarket.
Shops close early in the evening.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "When food is on special offer in the supermarket, it is easy to fill the basket with more than we need".

questions.q: Which tip is NOT mentioned in the text?
questions.explain: Bài có nhắc kiểm tra tủ lạnh, cấp đông bánh mì và trái cây, ăn đồ thừa hôm sau; không hề nói đến việc tự trồng rau.

readings.title: Science for Everyone: Citizen Scientists
readings.summaryVi: Người bình thường có thể giúp các nhà khoa học đếm chim, phân loại thiên hà hay ghi lại thời tiết – đó là khoa học công dân, với nhiều kết quả thật và lợi ích cho cả người tham gia.
readings.summaryEn: Ordinary people can help scientists count birds, classify galaxies or record the weather – this is citizen science, with many real results and benefits for the volunteers too.
readings.text:
You do not need a laboratory or a university degree to help scientists. Today, thousands of ordinary people take part in research projects in their free time. This is called citizen science.

The idea is simple. Scientists often need to collect a lot of information, but they do not have enough time or staff to do it alone. Volunteers can help by counting birds in their garden, taking photos of insects or measuring rainfall. Many projects use a mobile phone app, so people can send their results in a few seconds.

Some projects do not even require you to go outside. On certain websites, volunteers look at pictures of distant galaxies and sort them into groups. Others read old handwritten weather records so that the data can be stored on computers. Computers are fast, but people are still better at some tasks, such as noticing unusual shapes.

Citizen science has already produced real results. Volunteers have discovered new planets, found rare plants and helped scientists understand how animals move when the climate changes. In one bird count, families recorded which birds visited their gardens over a single weekend, and the results showed that some species were becoming less common.

There are benefits for the volunteers too. Many say that they learn new skills and feel more connected to nature. Children who join projects often become more interested in science at school.

Of course, there are some challenges. Volunteers sometimes make mistakes, so scientists must check the data carefully. Even so, most researchers agree that citizen science is a valuable way to involve the public in discovery.

questions.q: Citizen scientists need a university degree.
questions.explain: Ngay câu đầu: "You do not need a laboratory or a university degree to help scientists" → FALSE.

questions.q: Volunteers have helped to discover new planets.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Volunteers have discovered new planets" → TRUE.

questions.q: Most citizen science projects pay volunteers a small fee.
questions.explain: Bài không nói gì về việc trả tiền cho tình nguyện viên → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why do scientists need help from volunteers?
options: They do not have enough time or staff to collect all the information.
questions.explain: Bài viết: scientists "do not have enough time or staff to do it alone".

questions.q: What must scientists do because volunteers sometimes make mistakes?
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Volunteers sometimes make mistakes, so scientists must check the data carefully".

readings.title: Working from Home: The New Normal?
readings.summaryVi: Làm việc từ xa giúp tiết kiệm thời gian đi lại và linh hoạt hơn, nhưng cũng gây cô đơn và khó tách công việc khỏi đời sống riêng; mô hình kết hợp đang trở nên phổ biến.
readings.summaryEn: Remote working saves commuting time and offers more flexibility, but it can also cause loneliness and make it hard to separate work from private life; hybrid models are becoming common.
readings.text:
Not long ago, working from home was a rare privilege. Most employees travelled to an office every morning and returned in the evening. In recent years, however, remote work has become normal for millions of people, thanks to fast internet connections and online meeting tools.

For many workers, the biggest advantage is time. Without a daily commute, they can save an hour or more each day, which they may spend with their families, doing exercise or simply sleeping longer. Remote work also gives people more flexibility. Parents can collect their children from school, and people who live far from big cities can apply for jobs that were once out of reach.

Employers can benefit as well. Some companies have moved to smaller offices and reduced their costs. Several surveys suggest that many staff are just as productive at home, and in some cases more productive, because there are fewer interruptions.

However, working from home is not perfect. Some people find it hard to separate their job from their private life, especially if they work at the kitchen table. They may answer emails late at night and feel that they are never really off duty. Others feel lonely and miss chatting with colleagues. Managers also worry that new employees learn more slowly when they cannot watch experienced staff at work.

Because of these problems, many organisations now use a hybrid model. Employees spend part of the week in the office for meetings and teamwork, and the rest at home for tasks that need concentration. This approach seems to combine the best of both worlds, although it requires careful planning.

In the end, remote work is likely to remain part of modern life. The challenge is to make sure that it supports both the company and the wellbeing of its workers.

questions.q: Working from home used to be common for most employees.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Not long ago, working from home was a rare privilege" – trước đây đó là đặc quyền hiếm hoi → FALSE.

questions.q: Some surveys suggest that people working at home can be more productive.
questions.explain: Bài viết: many staff are "just as productive at home, and in some cases more productive" → TRUE.

questions.q: Most companies plan to close their offices completely.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói một số công ty chuyển sang văn phòng nhỏ hơn, không nhắc đến việc đóng cửa hoàn toàn → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Which problem of remote work is mentioned in the text?
options: Employees spend too much money on travel.
Some people find it hard to separate work from private life.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Some people find it hard to separate their job from their private life".

questions.q: What is a hybrid model?
options: Spending part of the week in the office and the rest at home
Sharing one job between two people
Working for a company in another country
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Employees spend part of the week in the office for meetings and teamwork, and the rest at home".

readings.title: Living with Less
readings.summaryVi: Lối sống tối giản – sở hữu ít đồ hơn – mang lại lợi ích về tiền bạc, tinh thần và môi trường, nhưng cũng bị phê phán là dễ dàng hơn với người giàu.
readings.summaryEn: Minimalism – owning fewer things – brings financial, mental and environmental benefits, but it is also criticised as easier for the wealthy.
readings.text:
Walk into the home of a minimalist and you may be surprised by how empty it looks. There might be a sofa, a table and a few books, but very little else. Minimalism is a lifestyle based on owning fewer things and focusing on what really matters.

The idea is not new. Many philosophers and religious traditions have taught that happiness does not come from possessions. However, minimalism has become especially popular in the last decade. Books and online videos show people clearing out their wardrobes and giving away boxes of items they no longer use.

Supporters say the benefits are both practical and emotional. A home with fewer objects is quicker to clean and easier to organise. People who buy less often save money, and some use these savings to travel or pay off debts. Many minimalists also report feeling calmer, because they spend less time looking after their belongings and less energy deciding what to buy.

There may be environmental benefits too. If people buy fewer products, factories need fewer raw materials, and less rubbish is created. Some minimalists choose to repair old items instead of replacing them, which helps to reduce waste.

Critics, however, point out some problems. They argue that minimalism can be easier for wealthy people, who can afford to throw things away and buy them again later if necessary. For families with low incomes, keeping extra items may be a sensible way to prepare for the future. Others feel that the style can become a fashion in itself, with people spending large sums on expensive "simple" furniture.

Perhaps the most useful lesson of minimalism is not to own as little as possible, but to think carefully before each purchase. Asking "Do I really need this?" can help anyone make wiser choices.

questions.q: Minimalism is a completely new idea.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "The idea is not new" – nhiều triết gia và truyền thống tôn giáo đã nói điều này từ lâu → FALSE.

questions.q: Some minimalists say that they feel calmer.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Many minimalists also report feeling calmer" → TRUE.

questions.q: Minimalists usually live in smaller homes than other people.
questions.explain: Bài không so sánh diện tích nhà của người theo lối sống tối giản với người khác → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why do critics say minimalism can be easier for wealthy people?
options: They do not need to clean.
They can afford to throw things away and buy them again later.
They read more books about it.
questions.explain: Bài viết: wealthy people "can afford to throw things away and buy them again later if necessary".

questions.q: What does the writer see as the most useful lesson of minimalism?
questions.explain: Bài viết: the lesson is "not to own as little as possible, but to think carefully before each purchase".

readings.title: The Hidden Cost of Cheap Clothes
readings.summaryVi: Thời trang nhanh giúp quần áo rẻ và hợp mốt, nhưng phải trả giá về nước, ô nhiễm, điều kiện lao động và lượng rác dệt may khổng lồ.
readings.summaryEn: Fast fashion makes clothes cheap and trendy, but the price is paid in water use, pollution, working conditions and huge amounts of textile waste.
readings.text:
A T-shirt that costs less than a sandwich sounds like a great deal. In the past twenty years, clothing has become cheaper and faster to produce than ever before. Large brands now release new designs every few weeks, encouraging shoppers to buy more often. This business model is known as fast fashion.

For consumers, the attraction is clear. Fast fashion allows people to follow the latest trends without spending much money. However, the low price on the label hides a number of other costs.

The first is environmental. The fashion industry uses enormous quantities of water; growing the cotton for a single pair of jeans can require thousands of litres. Dyeing fabric can pollute rivers if factories do not treat their wastewater. In addition, many cheap garments are made from synthetic materials such as polyester, which is produced from oil and sheds tiny fibres when it is washed.

The second cost is human. To keep prices low, some brands rely on factories where workers earn very low wages and work long hours. Safety standards in some buildings have been poor, and serious accidents have drawn global attention to the issue.

Finally, there is the problem of what happens to unwanted clothes. Because cheap items are often worn only a few times, a huge amount ends up in landfill or is shipped abroad. Only a small proportion of textiles is recycled into new clothing.

Some changes are taking place. Second-hand shopping has become fashionable among young people, and a number of brands now offer repair services or collect old garments. Shoppers can also help by choosing quality over quantity and asking where and how their clothes are made.

questions.q: Large fast-fashion brands release new designs only once a year.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Large brands now release new designs every few weeks" → FALSE.

questions.q: Polyester is made from oil.
questions.explain: Bài viết: polyester "is produced from oil" → TRUE.

questions.q: Most second-hand shops are run by charities.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói mua đồ cũ trở nên thời thượng với giới trẻ, không nhắc ai điều hành các cửa hàng đó → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: According to the text, why might dyeing fabric harm rivers?
options: Factories may not treat their wastewater.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Dyeing fabric can pollute rivers if factories do not treat their wastewater".

questions.q: What happens to many cheap clothes after they are worn a few times?
options: They are always recycled into new clothes.
They end up in landfill or are shipped abroad.
They are sent back to the factory.
They are repaired by the brands.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "a huge amount ends up in landfill or is shipped abroad".

readings.title: The Gig Economy: Freedom or Insecurity?
readings.summaryVi: Kinh tế việc làm tự do qua ứng dụng mang lại sự linh hoạt nhưng thiếu bảo hiểm, lương hưu và thu nhập ổn định; các chính phủ đang tìm cách cân bằng giữa hiệu quả và an toàn cho người lao động.
readings.summaryEn: The app-based gig economy offers flexibility but lacks insurance, pensions and a stable income; governments are looking for a balance between efficiency and protection for workers.
readings.text:
In many cities, the person who delivers your dinner, drives you home or assembles your new furniture may not be an employee of any company. Instead, they are likely to be part of the so-called gig economy, in which individuals take on short-term tasks through digital platforms and are paid separately for each job.

Advocates of this model emphasise its flexibility. Workers can, in theory, choose when and how much they work, logging on to an app for a few hours in the evening or at weekends. For students, carers and people seeking a second source of income, this freedom can be extremely valuable. Platforms also lower the barriers to entering the labour market: a person with a bicycle and a smartphone can begin earning almost immediately, without a formal interview.

Yet the arrangement has attracted growing criticism. Because most gig workers are classified as self-employed contractors rather than employees, they are generally not entitled to sick pay, holiday pay or a pension. Their income can be highly unpredictable, rising and falling with customer demand, the weather and changes to the app's pricing. Critics also point out that the flexibility may be less real than it seems. Algorithms often reward workers who accept every job and penalise those who decline, which puts pressure on drivers and couriers to remain online for long periods.

Governments have responded in different ways. Courts in several countries have ruled that some platform workers should be treated as employees, giving them the right to a minimum wage. Other policymakers favour a third category, which would offer basic protections while preserving the independence that many workers say they value. Platforms, for their part, argue that strict regulation would raise prices for consumers and reduce the number of available jobs.

The debate reflects a wider question about the future of work. As technology makes it easier to divide labour into small, separate tasks, societies must decide how to balance economic efficiency with security for the people who perform those tasks. There is unlikely to be a single solution, but the outcome will shape the working lives of millions.

questions.q: Gig workers are paid separately for each task.
questions.explain: Bài viết: individuals "are paid separately for each job" → TRUE.

questions.q: Most gig workers receive holiday pay.
questions.explain: Bài viết: gig workers "are generally not entitled to sick pay, holiday pay or a pension" → FALSE.

questions.q: The majority of gig workers are university students.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nêu sinh viên là một nhóm có thể hưởng lợi, không cho biết tỉ lệ sinh viên trong lực lượng này → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why might the flexibility of gig work be "less real than it seems"?
options: Apps only work in the evening.
Algorithms may penalise workers who decline jobs.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Algorithms often reward workers who accept every job and penalise those who decline".

questions.q: What do platforms argue about strict regulation?
options: It would raise prices and reduce the number of available jobs.
It would create a third category of worker.
questions.explain: Bài viết: platforms argue that strict regulation "would raise prices for consumers and reduce the number of available jobs".

readings.title: Can We Rebuild Coral Reefs?
readings.summaryVi: Rạn san hô đang suy giảm nghiêm trọng do nước biển nóng lên; các nhà khoa học thử trồng, nhân giống và “gọi cá” về rạn, nhưng giải pháp gốc rễ vẫn là cắt giảm khí thải.
readings.summaryEn: Coral reefs are declining sharply as the sea warms; scientists are trying to plant and breed coral and to "call" fish back to the reefs, but the root solution is still cutting emissions.
readings.text:
Coral reefs cover less than one per cent of the ocean floor, yet they support around a quarter of all marine species. They also protect coastlines from storms and provide food and income for hundreds of millions of people. Unfortunately, reefs are in serious decline, and scientists are now experimenting with ways to help them recover.

The main threat is rising sea temperature. Corals live in partnership with tiny algae that supply them with energy and give them their colour. When the water becomes too warm for a prolonged period, the corals expel the algae and turn white, a process known as bleaching. If temperatures return to normal quickly, the coral may survive; if not, it often dies. Pollution, overfishing and damage from boats and anchors add further pressure.

One of the most common restoration methods is coral gardening. Divers collect small fragments of healthy coral and grow them on underwater frames or ropes, where they are protected and monitored. Once the fragments have grown large enough, they are transplanted onto damaged sections of reef. Some projects have also discovered that breaking coral into very small pieces can make it grow much faster than normal, a technique called micro-fragmenting.

Other researchers are trying to breed corals that can tolerate higher temperatures. By selecting colonies that survived previous heatwaves and crossing them in laboratories, they hope to produce offspring that are more resilient. Some teams are even using underwater speakers to play the sounds of a healthy reef, which appears to attract young fish to degraded areas.

Despite these innovations, many marine biologists warn that restoration alone cannot save reefs. The area that can realistically be replanted is tiny compared with the scale of the damage, and restored coral will still be vulnerable if the oceans continue to warm. In their view, restoration should be seen as a way of buying time, while the fundamental solution lies in cutting greenhouse gas emissions.

Nevertheless, restoration projects offer real local benefits, such as supporting tourism and fisheries, and they raise public awareness. For communities that depend on reefs, even small successes can make a significant difference.

questions.q: Coral reefs cover about a quarter of the ocean floor.
questions.explain: Rạn san hô chỉ chiếm "less than one per cent of the ocean floor"; con số một phần tư là tỉ lệ loài sinh vật biển mà chúng nuôi dưỡng → FALSE.

questions.q: Bleaching happens when corals expel the algae that live with them.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the corals expel the algae and turn white, a process known as bleaching" → TRUE.

questions.q: Micro-fragmenting has been banned in some countries.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ giới thiệu kỹ thuật micro-fragmenting, không nói nước nào cấm → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What is the purpose of playing reef sounds underwater?
options: To attract young fish to degraded areas
questions.explain: Bài viết: âm thanh của một rạn san hô khỏe mạnh "appears to attract young fish to degraded areas".

questions.q: What do many marine biologists believe?
options: Restoration can fully replace lost reefs.
Coral gardening is too expensive to continue.
Restoration buys time, but cutting emissions is the real solution.
questions.explain: Bài viết: restoration is "a way of buying time, while the fundamental solution lies in cutting greenhouse gas emissions".

readings.title: Winning in the Mind: Sports Psychology
readings.summaryVi: Ở đỉnh cao thể thao, yếu tố tâm lý thường quyết định thắng thua: hình dung, kiểm soát lo âu, tự nhủ tích cực, động lực và sức khỏe tinh thần.
readings.summaryEn: At the top level of sport, the mental side often decides who wins: visualisation, controlling anxiety, positive self-talk, motivation and mental health.
readings.text:
At the highest level of sport, the physical differences between competitors are often extremely small. Elite athletes train for similar hours, follow similar diets and use similar equipment. What frequently separates a champion from the rest of the field is not strength or speed, but mental preparation. This is the territory of sports psychology.

One of the most widely used techniques is visualisation. Before a race or match, athletes imagine themselves performing each movement successfully, often in great detail. Research suggests that this mental rehearsal activates some of the same areas of the brain as physical practice, helping to strengthen the patterns needed during competition. Divers and gymnasts, for example, may mentally run through a routine dozens of times before attempting it.

Another key area is the management of anxiety. A certain level of nervousness can sharpen attention, but too much may cause muscles to tense and decisions to become rushed. Psychologists teach breathing exercises and short routines to help athletes stay calm under pressure. A tennis player who bounces the ball the same number of times before every serve is using a routine to focus the mind and block out distractions.

Self-talk is also important. Athletes are encouraged to notice negative thoughts, such as "I always miss this shot", and replace them with more constructive statements. Studies have found that positive or instructional self-talk can improve performance, particularly in tasks requiring precision.

Sports psychologists pay close attention to motivation as well. Athletes who focus on improving their own performance, rather than only on winning, tend to cope better with setbacks and are less likely to give up. Setting specific, achievable goals for each training session can help maintain this focus over a long season.

Increasingly, the field also addresses mental health more broadly. Several high-profile athletes have spoken openly about depression and burnout, encouraging teams to provide psychological support rather than treating such problems as signs of weakness. As a result, sports psychology is no longer seen as an optional extra but as an essential part of preparing for competition.

questions.q: Elite athletes usually differ greatly in their physical abilities.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the physical differences between competitors are often extremely small" → FALSE.

questions.q: A certain amount of nervousness can help athletes concentrate.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "A certain level of nervousness can sharpen attention" → TRUE.

questions.q: Visualisation works better for team sports than for individual sports.
questions.explain: Bài không so sánh hiệu quả của kỹ thuật hình dung giữa môn đồng đội và môn cá nhân → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why might a tennis player bounce the ball the same number of times before every serve?
options: To use a routine that focuses the mind
questions.explain: Bài viết: the player "is using a routine to focus the mind and block out distractions".

questions.q: According to the text, athletes who focus on improving their own performance…
questions.explain: Bài viết: they "tend to cope better with setbacks and are less likely to give up".

readings.title: A Thirsty Planet: Managing Water Scarcity
readings.summaryVi: Nước ngọt dễ tiếp cận rất hạn chế trong khi nhu cầu tăng nhanh; tưới nhỏ giọt, sửa đường ống, tái sử dụng nước thải, khử mặn và chính sách giá là những giải pháp đang được áp dụng.
readings.summaryEn: Easily accessible fresh water is very limited while demand is rising fast; drip irrigation, fixing leaking pipes, reusing wastewater, desalination and pricing policies are some of the solutions being used.
readings.text:
Water covers most of the Earth's surface, so it may seem strange that scarcity is one of the most pressing problems of the century. The difficulty is that only a tiny fraction of the planet's water is fresh and easily accessible; the rest is salty or locked in ice. As populations grow and economies develop, demand for this limited supply is rising quickly.

Agriculture is by far the largest user, accounting for roughly 70 per cent of the fresh water withdrawn worldwide. Irrigation allows farmers to grow crops in dry regions, but inefficient methods, such as flooding entire fields, lose large quantities through evaporation. Industry and growing cities place further demands on rivers and underground reserves. In some regions, groundwater is being pumped out far faster than rain can replace it, causing water tables to fall and, in certain cities, the ground itself to sink.

Climate change is adding to the pressure. Rising temperatures increase evaporation, and changing rainfall patterns mean that some areas experience longer droughts, while others suffer intense floods that are difficult to capture and store. Communities that rely on glaciers for their summer water supply face particular uncertainty as the ice retreats.

There is, however, considerable scope for improvement. Drip irrigation, which delivers water directly to the roots of plants, can significantly reduce consumption on farms. Many cities lose a large share of their treated water through leaking pipes, so repairing infrastructure can save enormous volumes. Wastewater, once regarded simply as a problem, is increasingly being treated and reused for irrigation, industry and even drinking. Coastal countries are also investing in desalination, which removes salt from seawater, although the process requires a great deal of energy and produces a salty by-product that must be disposed of carefully.

Pricing is another tool, though a controversial one. Economists argue that when water is very cheap, people have little incentive to conserve it. Critics respond that access to clean water is a human right and that higher charges could harm the poorest households. Many governments therefore use tiered systems, in which a basic quantity is provided at low cost and heavy users pay more.

Ultimately, managing water scarcity will require cooperation between farmers, industries, city authorities and neighbouring countries that share the same rivers.

questions.q: Agriculture uses about 70 per cent of the fresh water taken worldwide.
questions.explain: Bài viết: agriculture accounts for "roughly 70 per cent of the fresh water withdrawn worldwide" → TRUE.

questions.q: Desalination needs very little energy.
questions.explain: Bài viết: the process "requires a great deal of energy" → FALSE.

questions.q: Drip irrigation is now used on most farms in the world.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói tưới nhỏ giọt có thể giảm lượng nước tiêu thụ, không cho biết mức độ phổ biến → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why do some economists support higher water prices?
options: Because water is a human right
Because very cheap water gives people little incentive to conserve it
questions.explain: Bài viết: "when water is very cheap, people have little incentive to conserve it".

questions.q: What is a tiered pricing system?
options: A basic quantity is cheap and heavy users pay more.
Everyone pays exactly the same price.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "a basic quantity is provided at low cost and heavy users pay more".

readings.title: How Smart Should a City Be?
readings.summaryVi: Thành phố thông minh dùng cảm biến và dữ liệu để điều phối giao thông, năng lượng, nước; nhưng cũng đặt ra vấn đề quyền riêng tư, an ninh mạng và sự công bằng.
readings.summaryEn: Smart cities use sensors and data to manage traffic, energy and water, but they also raise concerns about privacy, cybersecurity and fairness.
readings.text:
Imagine a city where streetlights dim automatically when no one is around, where bins send a message when they need emptying, and where traffic signals adjust to the flow of cars in real time. This is the vision of the smart city: an urban area that uses sensors, data and digital networks to run services more efficiently.

Transport is often the first area to benefit. By analysing information from cameras, mobile phones and public transport cards, city authorities can identify where congestion builds up and change the timing of traffic lights accordingly. Some cities provide apps that show exactly when the next bus will arrive or where free parking spaces can be found, reducing the time drivers spend circling the streets.

Energy and resources are another focus. Smart meters allow households to monitor their electricity use, while sensors in water pipes can detect leaks before they become serious. Lighting systems that respond to movement can significantly cut the energy consumed by street lamps. Supporters argue that these improvements not only save money but also help cities meet their environmental targets.

However, the smart city raises important concerns. The most widely discussed is privacy. When cameras, sensors and apps constantly gather information about people's movements, there is a risk that this data could be misused, sold or stolen. Citizens may not know what is being collected or who has access to it. Security is a related issue: if essential systems such as traffic control or water supply are connected to the internet, they could become targets for hackers.

There is also a question of fairness. Expensive technology projects might concentrate on wealthy districts, leaving poorer neighbourhoods behind. People who do not own smartphones or are not comfortable with digital services, who are often older, may find it harder to use public services that move online.

For these reasons, many experts argue that a truly smart city is not simply one with the most technology. Instead, it is one that uses technology transparently, protects personal data and involves citizens in decisions about how their city should develop. Technology, in this view, should be a tool to serve people rather than an end in itself.

questions.q: In a smart city, traffic signals can change according to the flow of cars.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "traffic signals adjust to the flow of cars in real time" → TRUE.

questions.q: Privacy is rarely discussed in debates about smart cities.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "The most widely discussed is privacy" – đây là mối lo được bàn nhiều nhất → FALSE.

questions.q: Most smart city projects are paid for by private companies.
questions.explain: Bài không đề cập nguồn tài trợ cho các dự án thành phố thông minh → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: How can apps reduce the time drivers spend circling the streets?
options: By showing where free parking spaces can be found
questions.explain: Bài viết: apps show "where free parking spaces can be found, reducing the time drivers spend circling the streets".

questions.q: According to many experts, a truly smart city is one that…
options: uses technology transparently and involves citizens in decisions.
questions.explain: Bài viết: it is one that "uses technology transparently, protects personal data and involves citizens in decisions".

readings.title: The Bilingual Brain
readings.summaryVi: Song ngữ từng bị cho là gây rối cho trẻ, nay lại được gắn với lợi ích nhận thức và trì hoãn triệu chứng sa sút trí tuệ – dù các nhà khoa học vẫn tranh luận về mức độ của những lợi ích này.
readings.summaryEn: Bilingualism was once thought to confuse children; it is now linked to cognitive benefits and to delaying the symptoms of dementia – although scientists still debate how large these benefits are.
readings.text:
For much of the twentieth century, many parents and teachers believed that learning two languages at once could confuse young children and delay their development. Today, that view has largely been reversed. A growing body of research suggests that bilingualism may bring a range of cognitive benefits, although scientists still disagree about how large these benefits are.

When a bilingual person speaks, both languages appear to be active in the brain at the same time, even if only one is being used. To avoid mixing them, the brain must constantly select the correct language and suppress the other. Some researchers believe that this regular mental exercise strengthens executive function, the set of skills we use to plan, switch between tasks and ignore distractions. In several experiments, bilingual children performed better than monolingual children on tasks that required them to change rules quickly.

Perhaps the most striking claims concern ageing. Studies in a number of countries have found that bilingual people who develop dementia tend to show symptoms several years later than monolingual people with similar levels of brain damage. One explanation is the idea of cognitive reserve: a lifetime of managing two languages may build extra connections that help the brain compensate for decline.

However, the picture is not entirely clear. Some large studies have failed to find any advantage in executive function, and critics argue that earlier research involved small samples or did not fully account for other factors, such as education, income or immigration background. There is also concern that studies showing positive results are more likely to be published than those that find nothing.

What is less controversial is that early childhood is an excellent time to acquire a second language, particularly its pronunciation. Children exposed to two languages from birth typically reach the main stages of language development at roughly the same ages as their monolingual peers. Their vocabulary in each separate language may be slightly smaller at first, but their total vocabulary across both languages is usually comparable.

Regardless of the debate about cognitive advantages, the practical and cultural benefits of speaking more than one language are undeniable. Bilingual people can communicate with a wider range of people, access different media and, in many careers, enjoy better employment opportunities.

questions.q: In the past, some people believed that learning two languages could delay children's development.
questions.explain: Bài viết: many believed learning two languages "could confuse young children and delay their development" → TRUE.

questions.q: All studies have found that bilingual people have better executive function.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Some large studies have failed to find any advantage in executive function" → FALSE.

questions.q: Bilingual children usually learn to read earlier than monolingual children.
questions.explain: Bài không đề cập thời điểm biết đọc của trẻ song ngữ → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: According to the text, what is "cognitive reserve"?
options: A second language learned in old age
Extra connections that may help the brain compensate for decline
questions.explain: Bài viết: managing two languages "may build extra connections that help the brain compensate for decline".

questions.q: Why do critics question earlier research?
options: It used small samples or ignored factors such as education and income.
questions.explain: Bài viết: earlier research "involved small samples or did not fully account for other factors, such as education, income or immigration background".

readings.title: Listening to Volcanoes
readings.summaryVi: Địa chấn kế, vệ tinh và đo khí giúp nhận ra dấu hiệu núi lửa sắp phun, nhưng dự báo vẫn khó; kế hoạch khẩn cấp và niềm tin của cộng đồng cũng quan trọng không kém công nghệ.
readings.summaryEn: Seismometers, satellites and gas measurements help detect signs that a volcano is about to erupt, but prediction is still difficult; emergency plans and community trust matter as much as technology.
readings.text:
Around 800 million people live within 100 kilometres of an active volcano. For them, the ability to predict an eruption can be a matter of life and death. Although scientists cannot yet say exactly when a volcano will erupt, modern monitoring techniques have greatly improved their ability to recognise the warning signs.

The most important tool is the seismometer, which detects vibrations in the ground. As magma rises towards the surface, it forces its way through rock, creating swarms of small earthquakes. A sudden increase in the number or strength of these tremors often indicates that molten rock is on the move. Experienced volcanologists can also distinguish between different types of signals, some of which are linked to the movement of gas and fluids rather than breaking rock.

Changes in the shape of the ground provide further clues. When magma accumulates beneath a volcano, the surface may swell by several centimetres or even metres. Satellites using radar can now measure these tiny changes over large areas, while GPS stations placed on the volcano's slopes record movements continuously. In addition, scientists measure the gases released from vents and cracks. A rise in sulphur dioxide, for example, may suggest that fresh magma is approaching the surface.

Despite these advances, forecasting remains difficult. Each volcano behaves differently, and many show signs of unrest for months or years without erupting. If authorities order an evacuation too early or too often, residents may lose trust in the warnings and refuse to leave next time. On the other hand, a delayed decision can be catastrophic. Scientists must therefore communicate uncertainty clearly, often using alert levels that indicate the degree of danger rather than precise dates.

Many of the world's most dangerous volcanoes are located in developing countries, where funding for monitoring equipment is limited. International cooperation, cheaper sensors and satellite data that is freely available have begun to narrow this gap. Even so, experts stress that technology is only part of the solution: clear emergency plans, education and trust between scientists and local communities are just as essential in reducing the risk to human life.

questions.q: Scientists can now predict the exact date of most eruptions.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "scientists cannot yet say exactly when a volcano will erupt" → FALSE.

questions.q: The ground above a volcano may swell when magma accumulates.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "When magma accumulates beneath a volcano, the surface may swell by several centimetres or even metres" → TRUE.

questions.q: Sulphur dioxide is the most dangerous gas released by volcanoes.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói lượng sulphur dioxide tăng có thể là dấu hiệu magma đang lên, không so sánh độ nguy hiểm của các loại khí → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why can frequent early evacuations be a problem?
options: They are too expensive for satellites.
Residents may lose trust in warnings and refuse to leave next time.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "residents may lose trust in the warnings and refuse to leave next time".

questions.q: Apart from technology, what do experts say is needed to reduce the risk?
options: Emergency plans, education and trust with local communities
A ban on tourism near volcanoes
questions.explain: Bài viết: "clear emergency plans, education and trust between scientists and local communities are just as essential".

readings.title: When Tourism Becomes Too Much
readings.summaryVi: Du lịch quá tải khiến phố cổ chật chội, giá thuê nhà tăng và thiên nhiên bị tổn hại; các nơi đang thử thuế du lịch, giới hạn khách và quảng bá điểm đến ít người biết.
readings.summaryEn: Overtourism crowds old town centres, pushes up rents and damages nature; destinations are trying tourist taxes, visitor limits and promoting lesser-known places.
readings.text:
Tourism is one of the world's largest industries, providing jobs and income in almost every country. Cheaper flights, online booking and social media have made it easier than ever to visit distant places. Yet in some of the most popular destinations, the sheer number of visitors has become a source of tension. The term "overtourism" is now used to describe situations in which tourism damages the quality of life of local people or the very places that attract visitors in the first place.

The effects are most visible in historic city centres. Narrow streets designed for pedestrians can become so crowded that local people struggle to walk to work. Shops that once sold everyday goods are replaced by souvenir stalls and fast-food outlets. In several cities, the growth of short-term holiday rentals has reduced the number of homes available to local families, pushing up rents and forcing some of them to move away. As a result, certain neighbourhoods risk turning into what critics call "theme parks" with few permanent inhabitants.

Natural sites face different pressures. Popular beaches, mountain trails and coral reefs can suffer from erosion, litter and disturbance to wildlife. In some places, a single photograph shared widely online has drawn crowds to locations that lack the infrastructure to cope.

Authorities have tried a variety of responses. Some cities have introduced tourist taxes, using the revenue to maintain public spaces. Others limit the number of cruise ships allowed to dock each day or require visitors to book in advance for famous attractions. A few destinations have restricted new holiday rentals in residential areas. Tourism boards are also promoting lesser-known regions and encouraging travel outside the peak season, in the hope of spreading visitors more evenly.

These measures are not without controversy. Businesses that depend on tourism worry that restrictions will reduce their income, and some argue that charging fees makes travel accessible only to the wealthy. Finding the right balance is not easy. However, most experts agree that the aim should not be to stop tourism, but to manage it so that it benefits both visitors and the communities who host them.

questions.q: Short-term holiday rentals have caused rents to rise in some cities.
questions.explain: Bài viết: the growth of short-term holiday rentals has reduced available homes, "pushing up rents" → TRUE.

questions.q: Overtourism only affects historic cities.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Natural sites face different pressures" – bãi biển, đường mòn, rạn san hô cũng bị ảnh hưởng → FALSE.

questions.q: Tourist taxes have reduced visitor numbers in most cities.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói tiền thuế được dùng để duy tu không gian công cộng, không nói thuế làm giảm lượng khách → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: How are tourism boards trying to spread visitors more evenly?
options: By raising the price of flights
By promoting lesser-known regions and travel outside the peak season
questions.explain: Bài viết: tourism boards are "promoting lesser-known regions and encouraging travel outside the peak season".

questions.q: What is the writer's main conclusion?
options: Tourism should be managed to benefit both visitors and host communities.
Tourism should be stopped in crowded cities.
Only wealthy people should be allowed to travel.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "the aim should not be to stop tourism, but to manage it so that it benefits both visitors and the communities who host them".

readings.title: Artificial Intelligence at the Bedside
readings.summaryVi: Trí tuệ nhân tạo đọc ảnh y khoa ngang chuyên gia, nhưng phụ thuộc dữ liệu huấn luyện, thiếu minh bạch và chưa rõ trách nhiệm; giới chuyên môn xem AI là trợ lý chứ không thay thế bác sĩ.
readings.summaryEn: Artificial intelligence can read medical images as well as specialists, but it depends on its training data, lacks transparency and leaves responsibility unclear; experts see AI as an assistant, not a replacement for doctors.
readings.text:
Few fields illustrate both the promise and the pitfalls of artificial intelligence as vividly as medicine. Algorithms trained on vast collections of medical images can now identify certain cancers, eye diseases and fractures with an accuracy that rivals, and occasionally surpasses, that of experienced specialists. Enthusiasts envisage a future in which AI relieves overstretched doctors of routine tasks, catches diseases earlier and extends high-quality diagnosis to regions where specialists are scarce.

The appeal is easy to understand. A radiologist may examine hundreds of scans in a single shift, and fatigue inevitably increases the risk of error. An algorithm does not tire, and it can be deployed to flag suspicious images for priority review, allowing human experts to concentrate their attention where it is most needed. Beyond imaging, machine-learning systems are being used to predict which hospital patients are at risk of sudden deterioration, to speed up the discovery of new drugs and to transcribe consultations so that clinicians spend less time on paperwork.

Nevertheless, translating impressive laboratory results into real clinical benefit has proved more difficult than early headlines suggested. An algorithm is only as reliable as the data on which it was trained. If those data come predominantly from one population, the system may perform poorly for patients of different ethnic backgrounds, ages or sexes, thereby reinforcing existing inequalities in care. Systems that perform well in the hospital where they were developed have, in several documented cases, deteriorated markedly when introduced elsewhere, owing to differences in equipment or patient populations.

Transparency poses a further challenge. Many advanced models operate as so-called "black boxes", producing a conclusion without a readily interpretable explanation. Clinicians may be reluctant to act on a recommendation they cannot scrutinise, and patients are entitled to understand how decisions about their care are reached. There is also the unresolved question of accountability: if an AI-assisted diagnosis proves wrong, it is not obvious whether responsibility lies with the doctor, the hospital or the developer.

For these reasons, most experts envisage AI as an assistant rather than a replacement. Studies suggest that the combination of human judgement and algorithmic support frequently outperforms either alone, provided that clinicians remain alert to the risk of automation bias, the tendency to accept a machine's output uncritically. Regulators, meanwhile, are developing frameworks that require rigorous testing across diverse populations and continuous monitoring after deployment.

The ultimate test of medical AI will not be its performance in controlled trials, but whether it measurably improves outcomes for patients while preserving the trust on which the relationship between doctor and patient depends.

questions.q: Some algorithms can identify certain diseases as accurately as experienced specialists.
questions.explain: Bài viết: algorithms identify some diseases "with an accuracy that rivals, and occasionally surpasses, that of experienced specialists" → TRUE.

questions.q: An AI system that works well in one hospital will perform equally well in every other hospital.
questions.explain: Bài viết: some systems "deteriorated markedly when introduced elsewhere" → FALSE.

questions.q: Most hospitals have already replaced radiologists with algorithms.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nêu quan điểm của giới chuyên môn rằng AI là trợ lý, không cho biết các bệnh viện đã thay thế bác sĩ hay chưa → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What is "automation bias"?
options: A preference for older medical equipment
Training data that comes from a single population
The tendency to accept a machine's output uncritically
Errors caused by fatigue during long shifts
questions.explain: Bài viết định nghĩa automation bias là "the tendency to accept a machine's output uncritically".

questions.q: Why might an algorithm reinforce inequalities in care?
options: It is too expensive for poorer hospitals.
Its training data may come mainly from one population.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "If those data come predominantly from one population, the system may perform poorly for patients of different ethnic backgrounds, ages or sexes".

readings.title: Beyond Silk: The Ancient Trade Routes of Asia
readings.summaryVi: Con đường tơ lụa thực chất là mạng lưới tuyến đường bộ và biển kéo dài hàng thế kỷ, truyền bá không chỉ hàng hóa mà cả tôn giáo, kỹ thuật làm giấy – và cả dịch bệnh.
readings.summaryEn: The Silk Road was really a network of land and sea routes lasting for centuries, spreading not only goods but also religions, papermaking – and even disease.
readings.text:
The term "Silk Road" conjures up images of camel caravans crossing deserts laden with precious fabric. The reality was considerably more complex. Rather than a single road, it was a shifting network of overland and maritime routes that, over roughly fifteen centuries, linked China with Central Asia, India, the Middle East and the Mediterranean. Silk was merely one commodity among many; spices, horses, paper, glass, precious metals and ceramics all changed hands along the way.

Strikingly, few merchants ever travelled the entire distance. Goods typically passed through a relay of traders, each covering a particular segment before selling to the next. Oasis cities such as Samarkand flourished as hubs where merchants rested, exchanged goods and gathered intelligence about prices and political conditions further along the route. This fragmented structure meant that prices multiplied with every transaction, which is partly why silk commanded such extraordinary value in Rome.

The significance of these routes, however, extended far beyond commerce. Ideas, technologies and beliefs travelled alongside merchandise. Buddhism spread from India into China via Central Asian trading communities, while papermaking techniques gradually moved westward, eventually transforming record-keeping and scholarship in the Islamic world and later in Europe. Musical instruments, artistic motifs and agricultural crops were similarly diffused, leaving traces that historians still detect in surviving artefacts.

Not every exchange was beneficial. Many historians believe that the trade networks facilitated the transmission of disease, most notoriously the plague that devastated Europe and parts of Asia in the fourteenth century. The very connectivity that enabled prosperity also rendered distant populations vulnerable to shared catastrophes.

The decline of the overland routes is often attributed to the expansion of European sea voyages from the late fifteenth century, which allowed goods to be transported in bulk more cheaply by ship. Yet scholars increasingly emphasise that maritime trade across the Indian Ocean had long been substantial, and that political fragmentation and conflict in Central Asia also played a role. The story, once again, resists simple explanations.

Today the Silk Road enjoys renewed prominence, not least because modern infrastructure projects deliberately invoke its legacy. Historians caution, however, against romanticising the past. The ancient routes were neither centrally planned nor consistently peaceful; their enduring importance lies instead in demonstrating how sustained contact between distant societies can reshape economies, cultures and even the course of history itself.

questions.q: Most merchants travelled the whole distance between China and the Mediterranean.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "few merchants ever travelled the entire distance" – hàng hóa được chuyển qua nhiều chặng thương nhân → FALSE.

questions.q: Papermaking techniques moved gradually westward along the trade routes.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "papermaking techniques gradually moved westward" → TRUE.

questions.q: Samarkand was the largest city on the Silk Road.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nêu Samarkand là một trung tâm phát triển mạnh, không so sánh quy mô với các thành phố khác → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why did silk become so valuable in Rome?
options: It was produced in very small quantities.
It was always transported by sea.
Prices multiplied with every transaction along the relay of traders.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "prices multiplied with every transaction, which is partly why silk commanded such extraordinary value in Rome".

questions.q: What does the writer say about the decline of the overland routes?
options: It had several causes, including conflict in Central Asia.
It was caused only by European sea voyages.
It was caused by the plague.
It happened suddenly in the tenth century.
questions.explain: Bài viết nói ngoài các chuyến đi biển của châu Âu, "political fragmentation and conflict in Central Asia also played a role".

readings.title: The Attention Economy
readings.summaryVi: Khi sự chú ý trở thành tài nguyên khan hiếm, các nền tảng số được thiết kế để giữ chân người dùng – gây phân mảnh sự tập trung và lan truyền tin sai; giải pháp bền vững có thể nằm ở mô hình kinh doanh.
readings.summaryEn: When attention becomes a scarce resource, digital platforms are designed to keep users hooked – fragmenting concentration and spreading misinformation; a lasting solution may lie in the business model.
readings.text:
In an age of information abundance, the scarce resource is no longer information itself but the human attention required to consume it. This insight, articulated by economists decades before the smartphone, underpins what is now termed the attention economy. Many of the most valuable companies in the world offer their core services free of charge; their revenue derives instead from capturing users' time and selling access to it, chiefly through advertising.

The commercial logic has profound consequences for design. If profit depends on engagement, platforms have a powerful incentive to maximise the time users spend on them. Features such as infinite scrolling, autoplaying videos and notifications delivered at unpredictable intervals have been criticised for exploiting well-documented psychological tendencies. Variable rewards, such as the uncertain prospect of a new message or a burst of approval, are known to be particularly compelling, a principle long familiar to designers of gambling machines.

Critics contend that the cumulative effect is a fragmentation of attention. Constant switching between tasks appears to impose a cognitive cost, reducing the capacity for the sustained, deep concentration on which complex reasoning and creative work depend. Some researchers have linked heavy social media use to anxiety and poor sleep, particularly among adolescents, although establishing causation remains notoriously difficult: it is plausible that people who are already anxious gravitate towards their screens.

Moreover, the content that captures attention most effectively is not necessarily the most accurate or valuable. Algorithms that prioritise engagement may inadvertently amplify sensational, divisive or misleading material, since such content provokes strong reactions. This dynamic has prompted concern about the health of public debate and the spread of misinformation.

Responses have emerged on several fronts. Some technology companies have introduced tools that allow users to monitor their screen time or disable certain features. Legislators in various jurisdictions are scrutinising design practices that may be manipulative, especially where children are concerned. At the individual level, a growing movement advocates "digital minimalism", which means deliberately limiting the role of technology to activities that genuinely serve one's values.

Yet framing the issue purely as a matter of individual willpower may be misguided. When some of the most sophisticated engineering in history is devoted to capturing attention, expecting each user to resist unaided seems unrealistic. A more durable solution may require rethinking the underlying business models, so that the commercial success of digital services is aligned with, rather than opposed to, the wellbeing of the people who use them.

questions.q: Many companies in the attention economy earn money mainly from advertising.
questions.explain: Bài viết: their revenue comes from "capturing users' time and selling access to it, chiefly through advertising" → TRUE.

questions.q: Researchers have proved that social media directly causes anxiety in adolescents.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "establishing causation remains notoriously difficult" – chưa chứng minh được quan hệ nhân quả → FALSE.

questions.q: Digital minimalism is more popular among older adults than among young people.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói phong trào này đang phát triển, không so sánh theo độ tuổi → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why are variable rewards described as compelling?
options: Their uncertainty makes them particularly attractive, as in gambling machines.
questions.explain: Bài viết: variable rewards are "particularly compelling, a principle long familiar to designers of gambling machines".

questions.q: What does the writer suggest in the final paragraph?
options: Users should simply show more willpower.
Business models may need to be rethought to align with users' wellbeing.
Smartphones should be banned for adults.
questions.explain: Bài viết: "A more durable solution may require rethinking the underlying business models".

readings.title: Rewilding: Letting Nature Take the Lead
readings.summaryVi: Tái hoang dã khôi phục các quá trình tự nhiên bằng cách đưa loài như hải ly, sói trở lại; cách tiếp cận này đầy tham vọng nhưng gây tranh cãi và cần sự đồng thuận của cộng đồng.
readings.summaryEn: Rewilding restores natural processes by bringing back species such as beavers and wolves; the approach is ambitious but controversial and needs the agreement of local communities.
readings.text:
For much of the twentieth century, nature conservation in many countries focused on protecting particular species or preserving landscapes in a carefully managed state. Rewilding represents a markedly different philosophy. Rather than intervening continually to maintain a fixed condition, it seeks to restore natural processes and then, as far as possible, allow ecosystems to regulate themselves.

Central to rewilding is the reintroduction of species that once shaped their environments but disappeared because of hunting or habitat loss. Large predators and so-called ecosystem engineers often attract the most attention. The beaver, for instance, builds dams that slow the flow of rivers, creating wetlands that store water, reduce downstream flooding and support a remarkable diversity of insects, birds and amphibians. Similarly, the return of grazing animals such as wild cattle or horses can create a patchwork of open ground and woodland that benefits a wide range of plants.

The most frequently cited example is the reintroduction of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in the 1990s. According to a widely publicised account, wolves reduced the number of elk and altered their behaviour, allowing riverside vegetation to recover, which in turn stabilised riverbanks. Subsequent research, however, has suggested that this "trophic cascade" was considerably more complex and less dramatic than popular versions implied, with factors such as human hunting and drought also playing significant roles. The episode serves as a reminder that ecological outcomes are rarely as tidy as compelling narratives suggest.

Rewilding is not without its detractors. Farmers sometimes fear that returning predators will attack livestock, and beavers can flood valuable agricultural land. Critics also question whether a "wild" state can meaningfully be defined in landscapes that have been shaped by humans for thousands of years. Which point in history, they ask, should serve as the baseline? Proponents generally respond that the aim is not to recreate a specific past, but to increase the complexity and resilience of ecosystems.

Practical success therefore depends as much on social acceptance as on ecology. Projects that compensate farmers for losses, involve local communities in planning and create opportunities in nature tourism tend to encounter less opposition. In densely populated regions, rewilding may take more modest forms, such as allowing rivers to follow their natural courses or leaving parts of farmland to regenerate naturally.

As biodiversity continues to decline globally, rewilding offers an ambitious, if contested, vision: one in which human beings act less as managers of nature and more as facilitators of its recovery.

questions.q: Rewilding aims to keep landscapes in a fixed, carefully managed state.
questions.explain: Bài viết: rewilding seeks to restore natural processes "rather than intervening continually to maintain a fixed condition" → FALSE.

questions.q: Later research suggested that the effects of wolves in Yellowstone were more complex than popular accounts claimed.
questions.explain: Bài viết: nghiên cứu sau này cho thấy "trophic cascade" ở Yellowstone "was considerably more complex and less dramatic than popular versions implied" → TRUE.

questions.q: Beavers have been reintroduced to every country in Europe.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ giải thích vai trò của hải ly, không nói chúng được đưa trở lại những quốc gia nào → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Why is the beaver described as an ecosystem engineer?
options: Its dams create wetlands that support many species.
questions.explain: Bài viết: beavers build dams, "creating wetlands that store water, reduce downstream flooding and support a remarkable diversity" of species.

questions.q: According to the text, which factor helps rewilding projects meet less opposition?
options: Keeping local people out of planning
Introducing as many predators as possible
questions.explain: Bài viết: "Projects that compensate farmers for losses, involve local communities in planning and create opportunities in nature tourism tend to encounter less opposition".

readings.title: The Curious Power of the Placebo
readings.summaryVi: Hiệu ứng giả dược cho thấy kỳ vọng và bối cảnh điều trị có thể tạo ra thay đổi sinh lý thật; mặt trái của nó là hiệu ứng nocebo, và giả dược không thể thay thế thuốc thật.
readings.summaryEn: The placebo effect shows that expectations and the treatment setting can cause real physical changes; its downside is the nocebo effect, and placebos cannot replace real medicine.
readings.text:
In clinical research, the placebo, an inert substance such as a sugar pill, has traditionally been regarded as little more than a methodological tool. By comparing a new drug with a placebo, researchers can determine whether any improvement is attributable to the medication itself. Yet the placebo effect, the genuine improvement that some patients experience after receiving an inactive treatment, has increasingly become an object of study in its own right.

The phenomenon is most pronounced for symptoms that are subjective and influenced by the brain, such as pain, nausea and fatigue. Brain-imaging studies have shown that when patients expect pain relief, regions associated with the body's own pain-control system become more active, and the release of natural painkilling chemicals can increase. In other words, expectation is not merely imaginary; it can produce measurable physiological changes.

Context appears to matter enormously. Experiments have found that injections tend to produce stronger placebo responses than pills, that two pills can outperform one, and that branded or more expensive-looking tablets may be more effective than plain ones. The manner of the practitioner also plays a part: patients treated by a warm, attentive clinician frequently report greater improvement than those receiving identical treatment in a brisk, impersonal manner.

Perhaps the most counterintuitive findings concern so-called open-label placebos. In several trials, patients with conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome were explicitly told that they were receiving inactive pills, yet many still reported significant relief. Researchers speculate that the ritual of taking medication, combined with a credible explanation of how placebos can work, may be sufficient to trigger beneficial responses, although these studies have generally been small.

The placebo effect has a less welcome counterpart: the nocebo effect, in which negative expectations produce real side effects. Participants warned about possible symptoms are more likely to experience them, even when they have been given an inactive substance. This poses a genuine dilemma for doctors, who are obliged to inform patients of risks while avoiding the unintended creation of symptoms.

It is important not to overstate the power of placebos. They do not shrink tumours or cure infections, and relying on them in place of effective treatment would be dangerous. Their relevance lies elsewhere. A clearer understanding of how expectation and context influence recovery could help clinicians communicate more effectively and design care that maximises the benefits of genuinely active treatments.

questions.q: Placebo effects are strongest for subjective symptoms such as pain and nausea.
questions.explain: Bài viết: the phenomenon "is most pronounced for symptoms that are subjective and influenced by the brain, such as pain, nausea and fatigue" → TRUE.

questions.q: Placebos can cure infections if patients believe in them.
questions.explain: Bài viết: placebos "do not shrink tumours or cure infections" → FALSE.

questions.q: Open-label placebos are now widely prescribed by family doctors.
questions.explain: Bài chỉ nói về một số thử nghiệm nhỏ, không đề cập việc bác sĩ gia đình kê đơn giả dược → NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What is the nocebo effect?
options: Real side effects caused by negative expectations
A type of injection used in trials
questions.explain: Bài viết: the nocebo effect is one "in which negative expectations produce real side effects".

questions.q: Which factor is said to strengthen the placebo response?
options: Taking one pill rather than two
questions.explain: Bài viết: "patients treated by a warm, attentive clinician frequently report greater improvement".

readings.title: Universal Basic Income: Utopia or Necessity?
readings.summaryVi: Thu nhập cơ bản phổ quát hứa hẹn xóa bỏ thủ tục rườm rà và “bẫy phúc lợi”, nhưng chi phí rất lớn; các thí điểm cho kết quả tích cực song chưa đủ để kết luận.
readings.summaryEn: A universal basic income promises to remove complicated paperwork and the "welfare trap", but it is very expensive; pilot schemes have shown positive results that are not yet enough to draw conclusions.
readings.text:
The proposal that every citizen should receive a regular cash payment from the state, regardless of employment or wealth, has a surprisingly long and varied intellectual history. Advocated at different times by radical reformers and free-market economists alike, universal basic income (UBI) has re-emerged in recent years as a response to concerns about automation, insecure work and the complexity of existing welfare systems.

Proponents advance several distinct arguments. First, because the payment is unconditional, it eliminates the bureaucracy involved in assessing eligibility, as well as the stigma that sometimes deters people from claiming support to which they are entitled. Second, it avoids the so-called welfare trap, whereby people who take on paid work lose benefits at such a rate that they gain little or nothing financially. Third, supporters contend that a guaranteed income floor would provide security in a labour market increasingly characterised by short-term contracts and, potentially, by the displacement of jobs through artificial intelligence.

Critics raise equally substantial objections. The most immediate is cost. A payment generous enough to live on, distributed to an entire adult population, would require large increases in taxation or the dismantling of other public services. If, conversely, the payment is set at a modest level, it may be insufficient to replace targeted benefits for people with disabilities or high housing costs, potentially leaving the most vulnerable worse off. Others worry that an unconditional income might weaken the incentive to work, although the strength of this effect is fiercely disputed.

Empirical evidence remains limited, partly because genuinely universal schemes have rarely been tested. Pilot projects in countries including Finland, Kenya and Canada have typically involved selected groups rather than whole populations, and for fixed periods. Their findings have nonetheless been instructive. Recipients have generally reported improved wellbeing and reduced stress, and most studies have found little evidence of a significant decline in employment. Sceptics point out, however, that temporary experiments cannot reveal how behaviour or prices might change if a payment were permanent and nationwide.

Ultimately, the debate about UBI reflects deeper disagreements about the purpose of the welfare state: whether it should primarily provide a safety net for those in need, or guarantee every citizen a baseline of economic independence.
